item.content:encoded:
Meta title: Typhoon Roasters coffee electric roaster startup checklist — installation, calibration, first batch

Meta title & description

Meta title: Typhoon Roasters coffee electric roaster startup checklist — installation, calibration, first batch

Meta description: Step‑by‑step electric commercial coffee roaster startup checklist for Typhoon Roasters coffee systems. Covers site preparation, delivery, installation requirements, calibration, staff training, and the first production batch.

Introduction: Why an Electric Roaster Startup Checklist Matters

Bringing a new electric commercial coffee roaster online is one of the biggest infrastructure moves a specialty café or roastery makes.

If you’re considering Typhoon Roasters coffee equipment, you’re likely weighing:

  • Electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roaster for your startup

  • Installation requirements and permitting

  • Timeline from delivery to first production batch

This checklist walks you step‑by‑step through a Typhoon Roasters startup — from order to your first sellable batch — so you know exactly what to plan for and who needs to be involved.

All technical specs and requirements referenced here are based on Typhoon Roasters equipment datasheets and service documentation accessed in 2024–2025, plus industry standards from the EPA, NFPA, and EU guidance. Always confirm final values with Typhoon and your local electrician/engineer before installation.

Step 1: Choose the Right Typhoon Electric Roaster for Your Startup

Before you think about site prep, you need the right machine size and throughput.

Typhoon’s fully electric, fluid‑bed lineup covers small specialty cafés up to industrial roasteries:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO

    • 2.5 kg nominal batch, up to ~15 kg/h throughput

    • Roast time: ~5–7 minutes per batch

    • Up to ~6–7 batches per hour thanks to fast back‑to‑back capability

    • Power: 3‑phase 380–400 V; energy use about 0.3 kWh per kg roasted

    • Source: Typhoon 2.5 PRO spec sheet

  • Typhoon 5 PRO

    • 5 kg nominal batch, ~30 kg/h throughput

    • Roast time: ~5–7 minutes

    • Same 3‑phase 380–400 V; ~0.3 kWh/kg

    • Source: Typhoon 5 PRO spec sheet

  • Typhoon 10 PRO

    • 10 kg nominal batch, ~60 kg/h throughput

    • 3‑phase 380–400 V; ~0.3 kWh/kg

    • New generation is ~25% smaller and ~20% lighter than the previous model

    • Source: Typhoon 10 PRO spec sheet

  • Typhoon 20 kg & 30 kg industrial

    • 20 kg: up to ~100 kg/h throughput, 67 kW connection power

    • 30 kg: up to ~180 kg/h throughput, 110 kW connection power

    • 3‑phase 380–400 V, ~0.3 kWh/kg

    • Sources: Typhoon 20 kg, Typhoon 30 kg

For a specialty café or small roastery, most owners choose:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO — compact commercial coffee roaster for small café volumes

  • Typhoon 5 PRO — fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small roastery or multi‑site chain

Typhoon’s team will help you model capacity and ROI, but a simple rule of thumb:

  • Estimate weekly roasted volume in kg

  • Divide by machine throughput (e.g., 15–30 kg/h for 2.5–5 PRO)

  • Check that you can comfortably hit volume in 2–3 production days/week

Step 2: Electric Roaster Installation Requirements (Before You Order)

Electric roasters simplify many things versus gas drum systems, but they are still industrial machines.

You should lock in power, space, and code compliance before placing your order.

2.1 Power and electrical connection (Typhoon 2.5–30 kg)

All Typhoon production models are fully electric and require 3‑phase 380–400 V supply.

Typical connection power per Typhoon spec sheets:

  • 2.5 PRO — ~25–30 kW (example range based on 0.3 kWh/kg at 15 kg/h plus controls)

  • 5 PRO — ~35–40 kW (example range; confirm with Typhoon datasheet)

  • 10 PRO — ~55–60 kW (example range; Typhoon lists 60 kg/h at 0.3 kWh/kg)

  • 20 kg — 67 kW connection power (per Typhoon 20 kg spec)

  • 30 kg — 110 kW connection power (per Typhoon 30 kg spec)

These kW figures are indicative examples derived from Typhoon’s throughput and energy‑use messaging. Always rely on the latest Typhoon datasheet for your exact model and version.

From connection power you can estimate full‑load current (amps):

  • Formula: A ≈ kW × 1000 / (√3 × V × power factor)

  • Assuming power factor ~0.95 and voltage 400 V

Indicative full‑load amps and breaker sizes:

  • 2.5 PRO (~30 kW)

    • ~46–50 A full‑load

    • Typical breaker provision: 63 A, 3‑pole

  • 5 PRO (~40 kW)

    • ~62–66 A full‑load

    • Typical breaker provision: 80–100 A, 3‑pole

  • 10 PRO (~60 kW)

    • ~93–99 A full‑load

    • Typical breaker provision: 125 A, 3‑pole

  • 20 kg (67 kW)

    • ~104–112 A full‑load

    • Typical breaker provision: 125–160 A, 3‑pole

  • 30 kg (110 kW)

    • ~171–184 A full‑load

    • Typical breaker provision: 200–250 A, 3‑pole

Cable and gland sizing should be specified by your licensed electrician based on:

  • National standards (e.g., NEC in the US, IEC / HD 60364 in the EU, AS/NZS 3000 in AU)

  • Derating factors (ambient temperature, cable run length, installation method)

Action items:

  • Share Typhoon’s official electrical datasheet with your electrician

  • Size breakers and cables with 20–25% headroom over full‑load amps

  • Plan for a dedicated 3‑phase circuit and proper earthing/grounding

2.2 Space, clearance, and foundations

Typhoon’s shop roasters are designed for compact café placement:

  • 2.5 PRO footprint: ~1800 × 1150 × 1650 mm (L×W×H)

  • 5 PRO footprint: ~2150 × 1300 × 1900 mm

  • Source: Typhoon 2.5 PRO, Typhoon 5 PRO

Typhoon typically recommends:

  • Minimum 6 m² of floor area for a 2.5–5 PRO installation

  • A hard, level surface capable of supporting machine weight

  • Clearance around the roaster to service doors, controls, and ducts

Other manufacturers give clearances that you can treat as best practice:

  • Diedrich IR Series: at least 18 inches (~45 cm) of clearance around roaster and ducting, with inspection by local fire authorities before use (Diedrich IR Installation Manual, 2017)

  • ROEST P3000: keep 80 cm clear on all sides and place on a hard, level surface (ROEST P3000 setup guide)

For Typhoon, a practical café/roastery guideline:

  • 0.8–1.0 m clearance around all sides for access and cleaning

  • Additional clearance and straight duct runs for exhaust and filtration

  • No flammable materials stored within local fire‑code clearances

2.3 Permits and fire/code compliance

Even with fully electric heating, coffee roasting is treated as a process emitting particulates and VOCs.

Key references:

  • EPA (US): coffee roasting emissions include particulate matter, VOCs, organic acids, and combustion products; control may be required based on throughput (EPA AP‑42, Section 9.13.2, 2020)

  • NFPA 1 & NFPA 30A (US): address fire safety and ventilation for commercial cooking and industrial processes

  • EU: national building codes plus directives on industrial emissions; local municipalities may have specific odour/smoke limits

Action items (pre‑order):

  • Check with your local building authority if roasting is allowed in your chosen zoning

  • Confirm any needs for fire inspection, mechanical permits, or air‑quality permits

  • Share Typhoon’s equipment spec and emissions‑control plan with inspectors early

Step 3: Site Preparation for Coffee Roaster Delivery

Once your order is placed, you have a clear window to prepare the site.

3.1 Physical access and delivery logistics

Typhoon’s production roasters are shipped on crates/pallets and need a safe route from truck to final position.

Prepare for:

  • Loading dock or street‑level delivery access

  • Pallet jack or forklift capability

  • Door widths and hallway turns wide enough for the crate size (check Typhoon’s crate dimensions)

  • Temporary removal of doors/thresholds if required

Follow best practices from manufacturers like ROEST:

  • Inspect packaging upon arrival and document any transport damage before signing (ROEST P3000 setup guide)

3.2 Electric roaster installation requirements (on site)

Before your Typhoon system arrives, your electrician should:

  • Install the dedicated 3‑phase breaker and cabling to the roaster location

  • Provide a properly rated disconnect switch adjacent to the machine

  • Verify grounding/earthing resistance meets national standards

  • Label the circuit per local electrical code

For safety, treat Typhoon like any industrial appliance:

  • Only qualified personnel should connect the roaster to mains power

  • Follow lock‑out/tag‑out procedures when working on electrical panels

3.3 Ventilation and emissions control planning

Electric fluid‑bed roasters still emit chaff, smoke, and odours from beans.

Typhoon explicitly notes that electric roasters do not require a gas afterburner, but do need filtration or other emissions control depending on local regulations.

Typhoon’s electrostatic air filter (ESP) is designed for their 10–30 kg roasters:

  • Captures up to 99.5% of fine particles and roasting emissions

  • Reduces visible smoke vented to atmosphere

  • Source: Typhoon Airfilter

Because specific exhaust volumes (CFM / m³/h) and duct diameters depend on each installation and roaster generation, treat the following as planning ranges only:

  • Shop roasters (2.5–5 PRO)

    • Exhaust flow: often in the 400–800 m³/h (235–470 CFM) range for small fluid‑bed systems

    • Duct diameter: typically 150–200 mm (6–8") round duct

    • Stack height: aim for 1–2 m above roofline to disperse odour (check local code)

  • Industrial roasters (10–30 kg)

    • Exhaust flow: often 1000–2500 m³/h (590–1470 CFM) depending on model and filters

    • Duct diameter: typically 200–300 mm (8–12") round duct

    • Stack and fan sizing should be engineered by a mechanical contractor

Filter types commonly used with electric roasters:

  • ESP (electrostatic precipitator) — like Typhoon’s Airfilter; high capture efficiency for PM and smoke; requires periodic cleaning of collector plates

  • Mechanical filters (MERV 13–16) — for particulate; may be combined with ESP

  • Activated carbon — for odour control; cartridges need replacement based on hours or pressure drop

Action items:

  • Request Typhoon’s installation and ventilation drawings for your specific model

  • Have a mechanical engineer size fans, ducting, and stack per local code

  • Plan filter cleaning intervals (e.g., ESP plate cleaning monthly, carbon every 6–12 months depending on usage)

Here's how typical Typhoon roaster throughputs compare to approximate exhaust planning ranges.

Step 4: Delivery, Positioning, and Initial Power‑Up

On delivery day your goal is safe placement and basic commissioning, not full production.

4.1 Inspect and position the roaster

When the Typhoon roaster arrives:

  1. Inspect the crate

    • Check for damage, tilt indicators, or broken strapping

    • Photograph any issues and notify Typhoon immediately

  2. Move to final position

    • Use a pallet jack or forklift operated by trained staff

    • Position on the prepared, level pad with planned clearances

  3. Remove packaging

    • Keep manuals, accessory kits, and spare parts in a safe, labeled area

    • Check that the transparent roasting chamber and panel glass are intact

Typhoon runs 48 quality tests and ~20 test roasts per machine before shipment (Typhoon service and equipment overview), but you still need to verify everything on site.

4.2 Electrical connection and safety checks

With the roaster in place, your electrician should:

  • Connect the factory‑supplied cable or terminal block per Typhoon manual

  • Verify phase sequencing, voltage, and grounding before energizing

  • Perform insulation resistance and earth continuity tests

Before the first power‑up:

  • Confirm emergency stop, door interlocks, and safety guards are unobstructed

  • Ensure exhaust ducts and filters are installed and free of obstructions

Then, with Typhoon support (remote or on‑site):

  • Power on the roaster from the dedicated disconnect

  • Check that the control screen, sensors, and motors initialize correctly

Step 5: Coffee Roaster Calibration Procedure (Sensors & Profiles)

Calibration is where you turn a safe machine into a predictable, repeatable roaster.

Typhoon’s philosophy, consistent with its blog guidance, is clear:

  • Don’t copy sample roaster curves 1:1 to production

  • Focus on sensory targets and heat application style, then translate to the Typhoon profile (Typhoon roast profile scaling)

5.1 Instruments and reference standards

For a robust calibration procedure, assemble:

  • Reference thermometer — calibrated digital thermometer, preferably with a certificate traceable to standards like EURAMET Calibration Guideline No. 8 (Euramet CG‑8)

  • Type K thermocouple probes — thin‑gauge (1–3 mm) for fast response if checking air/bean temps

  • Data logging — either Typhoon’s built‑in logging or an external logger to record temperature and RoR

5.2 Sensor verification (dry run)

Perform a dry‑run calibration before roasting any coffee:

  1. Ambient check

    • Compare the roaster’s ambient sensor reading with your reference thermometer placed near the bean hopper

    • Acceptable difference: within ±1–2 °C

  2. Air temperature check

    • Run the roaster with no beans and ramp to a moderate setpoint (e.g., 150–180 °C)

    • Insert the reference thermocouple into the exhaust or designated test port (follow Typhoon’s service instructions)

    • Compare controller reading vs reference; aim for ±3–5 °C agreement

  3. Bean probe check (if applicable)

    • Load a small test batch (e.g., 1–2 kg) and record the curve

    • Use your reference probe placed as close as safely possible to the bean mass to compare trends rather than exact values

Record:

  • Any consistent offsets (e.g., roaster reads 3 °C higher than reference at 180 °C)

  • RoR behaviour (steady, noisy, lagging)

If offsets exceed tolerances:

  • Contact Typhoon support; they may guide you through software offset adjustments or hardware inspection

5.3 Baseline profile creation

Create one baseline profile per core product (e.g., espresso, filter, dark roast):

  1. Choose a green lot you know well from your previous roaster

  2. Set a conservative profile on the Typhoon (medium charge temp, moderate gas equivalent / power, standard airflow)

  3. Roast a small batch and cup it the next day

  4. Adjust development time, heat ramps, and airflow to hit your familiar flavour target

Document:

  • Target color (Agtron), end temperature, and development time %

  • Typhoon power and airflow steps

  • Sensory notes

This becomes your reference profile to clone and tweak.

Step 6: Roastmaster Training & Staff Onboarding

Typhoon treats installation, calibration, and training as one integrated launch process.

Per Typhoon’s service documentation, every installation includes:

  • Complimentary Roastmaster training course during startup/calibration

  • Access to a complete online roasting course

  • Ongoing support covering installation, maintenance, and training (Typhoon service)

6.1 How to train staff on a coffee roasting machine

Your internal training plan should cover four areas:

  1. Safety and compliance

    • Emergency stop, safe shutdown, and lock‑out/tag‑out

    • Fire extinguisher use and evacuation routes

    • Housekeeping: chaff removal, dust control, clear access to ducts and filters

  2. Basic operation

    • Loading beans and setting batch size

    • Selecting and running saved profiles

    • Monitoring the roast curve and key milestones (dry end, first crack, drop)

  3. Quality control

    • Sample roasting and cupping protocol

    • Logging roast parameters, cupping scores, and defects

    • Adjusting profiles in Typhoon software based on sensory feedback

  4. Maintenance and cleaning

    • Daily: vacuum chaff collector, wipe chamber, check filters

    • Weekly: deeper clean of ducts, inspect seals, verify sensor attachments

    • ESP/filters: clean plates and replace media as scheduled

Typhoon’s automation and recipe storage make it easier to train new roasters:

  • Your lead roastmaster sets profiles and QC standards

  • Junior staff focus on loading, monitoring, and logging, not manual heat juggling

Step 7: First Production Batch Roastery Checklist

With installation complete, sensors verified, and staff trained, you’re ready for the first production batch.

Use this pre‑flight checklist before roasting coffee you plan to sell:

7.1 Pre‑roast checks

  • Power & safety

    • Main disconnect ON, no alarms on the control screen

    • Emergency stop switches tested and functional

  • Ventilation & filtration

    • Exhaust fan running, proper airflow confirmed

    • ESP / filters clean and correctly installed

    • Duct dampers in correct position

  • Cleanliness

    • Chamber free of debris

    • Chaff collector empty

    • Surrounding area clear of combustible clutter

7.2 Running the first production batch

  1. Select your baseline profile for the chosen coffee

  2. Load the target batch size (respecting Typhoon’s recommended max load)

  3. Monitor the roast curve and sensory markers

  4. At drop, cool and package separately as “Batch 1 – reference”

  5. Record all key parameters:

    • Charge temp and time

    • First crack time and temperature

    • Drop temp, time, and development %

    • Exhaust temperature and ESP performance

Cup Batch 1 the following day:

  • Compare flavour to your target profile from your previous roaster

  • Adjust profile if needed (earlier/later development, airflow changes)

  • Once you’re satisfied, lock the profile and roll into full production

Typhoon’s fast back‑to‑back roasting (no dedicated cool‑down cycle) allows you to ramp quickly:

  • For 2.5–5 PRO, plan up to 6–7 batches per hour at full capacity

  • For 10–30 kg, maintain continuous production up to 60–180 kg/h per Typhoon specs

Electric Coffee Roaster vs Gas Drum Roaster Startup Comparison

For startups comparing electric roaster vs gas drum roastery paths, the checklist above highlights key differences.

8.1 What’s simpler with electric Typhoon systems

  • No gas lines or burners

    • Avoid gas‑line installation, pressure regulators, and combustion tuning

    • Fewer fire‑hazard points and simpler inspections

  • Lower, more predictable energy use

    • Typhoon cites about 0.3 kWh/kg roasted across its line, often ~3× less energy per kg than traditional setups (based on Typhoon’s energy‑efficiency messaging)

    • Easier to model operating costs and ROI

  • Flexible siting

    • 3‑phase 380–400 V supply is common in commercial and light‑industrial spaces in Europe and many other markets

    • Compact installations (e.g., 6 m²) make in‑café roasting realistic

8.2 What remains similar to gas drum startups

  • Emissions planning

    • EPA and local authorities still treat roasting as a source of PM and VOCs

    • You need ducts, fans, and filtration either way

  • Permits and inspections

    • Building, mechanical, and fire permits often apply equally to gas and electric

    • Local fire inspector may need to sign off on completed installation (Diedrich explicitly requires this for gas; it’s good practice for electric too)

  • Calibration and training

    • Sensors still need verification against reference standards

    • Staff still require safety and QC training

Overall, a Typhoon electric system is usually faster to bring online (no gas infrastructure) and more efficient in energy use, while still requiring serious planning for ventilation, emissions, and safety.

Conclusion: 100% Convection, 0% Compromise — Ready for Your First Batch

Following this electric roaster startup checklist, most Typhoon Roasters coffee customers move from delivery to first production batch within days, not weeks:

  • Site prep ensures power, ventilation, and code compliance are ready

  • Delivery and installation get the machine safely online

  • Calibration and training make your profiles repeatable and your team confident

For a specialty café or growing roastery, Typhoon’s fully electric, fluid‑bed platform offers:

  • Twice the output, half the hassle versus many comparable drum systems

  • Electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roastery startup comparison that favours lower complexity and higher sustainability

  • A visible, theatre‑ready roaster that becomes part of your brand story

If you’re planning a new roastery or upgrading your café into a production hub, Typhoon’s team can help you work through this checklist for your exact site and market.

FAQ: Typhoon Roasters Coffee Startup Questions

Is a Typhoon Roasters coffee roaster ideal for a small café?

Yes. The Typhoon 2.5 PRO and 5 PRO are designed as compact commercial coffee roasters for small cafés and micro‑roasteries.

Key advantages for cafés:

  • Small footprint (~6 m² installation space) and transparent roasting chamber make roasting an in‑store experience

  • Fully electric — no gas lines or burners

  • Fast roast cycles (~5–7 minutes) and up to 6–7 batches per hour

This combination makes Typhoon one of the best electric coffee roaster options for specialty cafés that want to roast on site.

How does an electric coffee roaster compare to a gas drum roastery for startups?

For startups, the electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roaster comparison usually comes down to:

  • Infrastructure: electric needs 3‑phase power; gas needs gas lines, regulators, and flues

  • Permits: both need ventilation and fire safety approvals; gas adds combustion‑related inspections

  • Efficiency: Typhoon’s ~0.3 kWh/kg use is often lower than many gas drum setups

If your space already has 3‑phase power or can be upgraded, going electric with Typhoon typically means faster installation, simpler permitting, and lower energy use.

What filtration or emissions control do I need for a Typhoon electric roaster?

Even with electric heating, you’ll need emissions control:

  • At minimum, a properly sized exhaust fan and duct venting above roofline

  • For urban or sensitive areas, an ESP filter like the Typhoon Airfilter plus mechanical filtration (MERV 13–16)

  • In some markets, activated carbon odour filters are recommended or required

Exact requirements depend on your local air‑quality regulations, throughput, and neighbours. Typhoon can provide recommended filtration packages per model, but final system design should be confirmed with a mechanical engineer and local authorities.

Are there noise or odour limits for electric commercial coffee roasters in the US, EU, and AU?

Most jurisdictions treat roasters under commercial noise and odour regulations rather than special coffee‑only rules.

Typical patterns:

  • US: city noise ordinances (dB limits by zone), plus EPA and state air‑quality rules for PM and VOCs

  • EU: national environmental acts and local bylaws governing noise and odour; stack heights and filtration often specified by municipalities

  • Australia: state EPA guidelines and local council rules for noise and cooking odours

Typhoon’s electric systems avoid burner noise, but fans and chaff collectors still produce sound. When in doubt, ask your local council or environmental agency for guidance on:

  • Maximum dB at property boundary

  • Odour complaints process and thresholds

Do I still need permits for an electric Typhoon roaster if I’m only roasting a few days per week?

Yes, in most cases.

Even small‑volume roasting usually requires at least:

  • Building / fit‑out permits for equipment installation

  • Mechanical permits for ducts and fans

  • Fire inspection for process safety

Some regions have thresholds below which formal air‑quality permits aren’t required, but you must still comply with general nuisance, odour, and fire safety laws.

Discuss your planned throughput (kg per day/week) with local authorities and share Typhoon’s datasheets early. This is often the fastest way to secure clear, written requirements.

For detailed Typhoon Roasters coffee startup equipment guidance, site‑specific electric roaster installation requirements, and fully electric commercial coffee roaster reviews from existing customers, reach out to Typhoon directly via their website. Their engineering and support team can help tailor this checklist to your café or roastery.

item.title: How to Finance Electric Commercial Coffee Roasters: A Practical Guide for Modern Roasteries
item.dc:creator: Typhoon Editorial
item.description: Upgrading to high‑end commercial roasting equipment is one of the biggest investments a specialty café or roastery will ever make.
item.content:encoded:
Upgrading to high‑end commercial roasting equipment is one of the biggest investments a specialty café or roastery will ever make.

Best electric commercial coffee roaster & fully electric commercial coffee roaster financing

Upgrading to high‑end commercial roasting equipment is one of the biggest investments a specialty café or roastery will ever make.

For many early‑stage and growing businesses, the question isn’t “Which is the best electric commercial coffee roaster?” but “How do we pay for it—and how fast does it pay us back?”

This guide breaks down practical funding and financing options for modern roasting equipment, with a focus on fully electric, commercial fluid‑bed coffee roasters like Typhoon Roasters.

We’ll cover:

  • Bank loans, SBA financing, and equipment loans (U.S. and beyond)

  • Leasing vs buying

  • Grants and incentive programs for energy‑efficient roasters

  • Example budgets for café‑scale and production‑scale setups

  • How Typhoon’s electric platform can strengthen lender and investor conversations

Electric coffee roaster vs gas drum: why financing looks different

When you compare an electric coffee roaster vs a gas drum roaster, you’re not just comparing hardware.

You’re comparing total installed cost, permitting risk, and operating efficiency—exactly the factors lenders and investors care about.

Electric vs gas: roastery startup comparison

Electric commercial roasters typically:

  • Eliminate gas lines and open flames
    Typhoon’s installation guide notes that their roasters are fully electric and do not require gas connections or burners, though they still need 3‑phase power and exhaust/odor control.[^typhoon-install]

  • Reduce installation complexity and site‑prep risk
    Bellwether Coffee estimates that installing an electric shop roaster can be USD $15,000–$40,000 cheaper than a similar gas drum roaster once you factor gas lines, ductwork, hoods, afterburners, and related construction. This is presented as an estimated range, based on typical U.S. café build‑outs.[^bellwether-cost]

  • Offer faster throughput at similar nominal capacity
    Typhoon’s electric fluid‑bed models, such as the 2.5 PRO (≈15 kg/h) and 5 PRO (≈30 kg/h), roast in about 5–7 minutes per batch with up to 6 batches/hour, reducing cool‑down bottlenecks compared with many gas drum roasters.[^typhoon-install]

  • Use less energy per kg roasted
    Typhoon cites an energy use of roughly 0.3 kWh/kg on compact models,[^typhoon-install] which they position as around 3× less energy per kg than typical drum roaster setups. This 3× figure is a vendor claim based on Typhoon’s internal comparisons, not an independent lab benchmark.

By contrast, traditional gas drum roasters often require:

  • Gas lines and safety inspections

  • Larger, hotter exhaust runs

  • Afterburners or catalysts for emissions in many urban jurisdictions

  • Longer roast and cool‑down cycles (commonly 10–15+ minutes per batch for similar capacities)

Side‑by‑side: electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roaster startup comparison

Below is a high‑level comparison useful in business plans and lender decks.

H3: Electric vs gas — key factors for roastery financing

  • Installation cost

    • Electric: lower site‑prep, no gas lines; Bellwether estimates $15k–$40k savings vs gas in typical U.S. installs.[^bellwether-cost]

    • Gas drum: higher construction costs for gas lines, venting, and emissions control.

  • Permits & timelines

    • Electric: focus on electrical capacity, basic exhaust, and building permits.

    • Gas drum: gas utility approvals, fire, mechanical, and sometimes environmental permits.

  • Energy use (per kg)

    • Electric fluid‑bed (Typhoon): vendor‑claimed ~0.3 kWh/kg.[^typhoon-install]

    • Gas drum: varies widely; many roasteries report higher kWh‑equivalent when you combine gas and auxiliary equipment.

  • Throughput & flexibility

    • Electric hot‑air systems (Typhoon, PROBAT P25e) emphasize fast heat response and minimal heat‑up/cool‑down penalties.[^typhoon-install][^probat-p25e]

    • Gas drum: more thermal inertia; fewer back‑to‑back batches per hour at the same batch size.

  • Footprint & in‑café roasting

    • Electric: easier to place inside cafés, with transparent roasting chambers becoming part of the brand experience.[^typhoon-install]

    • Gas drum: larger footprints and emissions often push roasting into back rooms or separate facilities.

Core financing options for high‑end commercial roasting equipment

Most roasteries fund equipment through a mix of:

  • Conventional bank loans

  • SBA‑backed loans (U.S. only)

  • Dedicated equipment financing

  • Leasing

  • Grants and incentives (mainly for energy efficiency)

1. Bank loans & equipment financing

Who it’s for: cafés and roasteries with solid credit and a clear expansion plan.

Examples:

  • Equipment loans (U.S.):
    Bank of America offers business equipment loans from USD $25,000 with terms up to 5 years, secured by business assets.[^bofa-equipment]

  • Standard term loans (global):
    Most banks in Europe, North America, and Asia offer term loans for machinery and fit‑out. Interest rates, collateral requirements, and terms vary by country.

Key features:

  • Fixed monthly payments

  • Ownership from day one

  • Often tied to personal guarantees for small businesses

Best use cases:

  • Funding one or more commercial fluid‑bed coffee roasters for a growing roastery

  • Bundling roasters, silos, packaging lines, and café build‑out into a single facility loan

2. SBA‑backed loans (U.S.‑specific)

For U.S. roasteries, SBA programs are often the backbone of the capital stack.

  • SBA 7(a) loans

    • Up to USD $5 million in loan amount[^sba-7a]

    • Can fund equipment plus working capital

    • Flexible use: roasters, inventory, marketing, and hiring

  • SBA 504 loans

    • Designed for fixed assets like machinery and real estate

    • Up to USD $5.5 million per project[^sba-7a]

    • Low down payments (often 10%) and long terms; Bank of America cites 10% down as typical.[^bofa-equipment]

  • New SBA rule (2026): combined 7(a)+504
    SBA announced that eligible borrowers can stack 7(a) and 504 to access up to USD $10 million in SBA‑backed financing.[^sba-7a]

Best use cases:

  • Building a roasting facility with 10–30 kg Typhoon industrial systems (e.g., Typhoon 20 kg at 100 kg/h or Typhoon 30 kg at 180 kg/h) plus green coffee inventory.[^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

Geography note: SBA programs are U.S.‑only. In the EU and UK, similar roles are played by national development banks and guarantee schemes, such as KfW in Germany, Bpifrance in France, and the British Business Bank in the UK. Terms and caps differ but the structure—public guarantees on commercial loans—is similar.

3. Leasing high‑end roasters

Leasing spreads the cost of equipment over time and may keep debt off the balance sheet, depending on accounting rules.

Common structures:

  • Operating leases
    Lower monthly payments, option to upgrade at end of term.

  • Finance leases
    Higher payments; you own the machine at lease end for a nominal buy‑out.

Pros:

  • Lower upfront cash outlay

  • Potentially easier approvals than bank loans

  • Flexibility to upgrade as capacity grows

Cons:

  • Total cost over the term may be higher than a purchase

  • Contract complexity (fees, insurance, maintenance)

Leasing is often attractive for:

  • Early‑stage specialty cafés adding a compact commercial coffee roaster for small café operations

  • Roasteries testing new locations or roasting volume before committing to full ownership

4. Grants, incentives & energy‑efficiency programs

Direct grants for coffee roasting equipment are limited, but energy‑efficient electric roasters can unlock programs designed for sustainability.

USDA REAP (U.S.‑specific, rural businesses)

The USDA Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) provides grants and guaranteed loans to rural small businesses making energy‑efficiency or renewable energy upgrades.[^usda-reap]

  • Energy efficiency grants:

    • Range USD $1,500–$250,000 per project[^usda-reap]

  • Renewable energy system grants:

    • Range USD $2,500–$500,000[^usda-reap]

  • Combined support:
    REAP grants plus guaranteed loans can cover up to 75% of eligible project costs.[^usda-reap]

An electric fluid‑bed coffee roaster with documented lower energy use (e.g., Typhoon’s ~0.3 kWh/kg claim) can be part of an energy‑efficiency project proposal.

Geography note: In the EU, similar support may come from national energy‑efficiency grants or EU structural funds; in the UK and Canada, regional green‑business or clean‑technology programs often play this role. Eligibility, grant sizes, and documentation requirements vary significantly.

5. Tax tools: Section 179 & bonus depreciation (U.S.)

Tax treatment can dramatically improve first‑year cash flow for U.S. roasteries.

  • Section 179 deduction
    For tax years beginning in 2026, the maximum Section 179 deduction is USD $2.56 million.[^irs-946]
    That means many roasteries can expense the full cost of roasters in year one, subject to income limits.

  • 100% first‑year bonus depreciation
    IRS guidance indicates 100% additional first‑year depreciation applies to eligible depreciable property acquired after January 19, 2025.[^irs-946]

Combined, these tools can reduce effective after‑tax cost of equipment, shortening the payback period.

Always confirm details with a local tax adviser; Section 179 and bonus rules apply only to U.S. taxpayers. Other countries use different accelerated depreciation schemes.

Example budgets: from specialty café to production roastery

Let’s look at simplified example budgets to show how Typhoon’s electric setup shapes lender and investor conversations.

All amounts below are in USD, for comparability. Local currency conversions should use up‑to‑date FX rates at the time of planning.

Scenario 1: Small specialty café with in‑house roasting

Goal: Install a compact commercial coffee roaster for small café operations—equivalent throughput to a 5 kg drum roaster but with lower energy use.

Equipment choice (example):

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO

    • Nominal capacity: 15 kg/h[^typhoon-install]

    • Roast time: 5–7 minutes per batch[^typhoon-install]

    • Energy use: ≈0.3 kWh/kg (vendor‑provided)[^typhoon-install]

    • Power: 380–400V, 3‑phase[^typhoon-install]

Indicative budget (U.S. urban café):

  • Roaster (assuming high‑end electric shop roaster price band similar to Bellwether’s $22,000–$27,000 MSRP for their 1.5 kg shop roaster[^bellwether-cost]):

    • Assume $25,000 for planning (exact Typhoon pricing depends on configuration and region).

  • Electrical upgrades to 3‑phase, modest exhaust and odor control:

    • Estimate $10,000–$20,000 (varies heavily by building; this is an estimated U.S. range).

  • Ancillary equipment (green bins, small destoner, packaging table):

    • $5,000–$10,000.

Total project envelope: ≈$40,000–$55,000.

Financing stack example:

  • Equipment loan: $35,000 over 5 years

  • Owner equity / cash: $5,000–$20,000

  • Potential local energy‑efficiency rebate: $0–$5,000

Scenario 2: Growing roastery targeting 100 kg/h

Goal: Upgrade to industrial‑scale electric roasting while maintaining specialty‑grade quality.

Equipment choice (example):

  • Typhoon 20 kg

    • Hourly capacity: 100 kg/h continuous production[^typhoon-20]

    • Power connection: 67 kW, 380–400V 3‑phase[^typhoon-20]

    • Vendor‑claimed energy use: ≈0.3 kWh/kg[^typhoon-20]

Indicative budget (production facility build‑out):

  • Roaster system (20 kg industrial): assume $120,000–$200,000 MSRP range for planning purposes, based on typical market pricing for high‑end 20–25 kg specialty roasters (Typhoon, PROBAT, Giesen, etc.). Actual Typhoon pricing varies by region and options.

  • Electrical infrastructure (high‑capacity 3‑phase, panel upgrades): $30,000–$60,000 (estimated range; heavily site‑dependent).

  • Ventilation, silos, green storage, packaging line: $80,000–$150,000.

Total project envelope: ≈$230,000–$410,000.

Financing stack example (U.S.):

  • SBA 504 loan: $200,000–$350,000 for equipment and facility upgrades[^sba-7a]

  • Owner equity: 10–20% of project cost

  • USDA REAP grant (if rural and eligible): potentially $50,000–$100,000 toward energy‑efficient upgrades[^usda-reap]

These numbers are planning tools, not quotes. They help investors visualize how electric roasting affects total installed cost and capital mix.

Best electric coffee roasters for specialty cafés (compact commercial recommendations)

If you’re looking for the best electric coffee roaster for a specialty café, focus on:

  • Throughput vs footprint

  • Energy use and operating cost

  • Ability to roast in front of guests

Compact commercial coffee roaster for small café use cases

Vendor‑provided examples:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO (electric fluid‑bed)

    • Suitable for cafés roasting 15 kg/h or less in‑house.[^typhoon-install]

    • Transparent roasting chamber for in‑store visibility.

    • 380–400V 3‑phase, 0.3 kWh/kg energy claim.[^typhoon-install]

  • Typhoon 5 PRO

    • 30 kg/h capacity and up to 6 batches/hour.[^typhoon-install]

    • Ideal for small roasteries or multi‑site café brands with centralized roasting.

Other electric options in the market (non‑Typhoon):

  • Bellwether Shop Roaster

    • MSRP $22,000 standalone or $27,000 with continuous roasting kit (pricing as of public Bellwether blog post).[^bellwether-cost]

    • Plugs into standard 220V outlet, no gas lines or construction required (vendor claim).[^bellwether-cost]

These systems illustrate how fully electric commercial coffee roaster reviews often highlight ease of installation and sustainability alongside roast quality.

Typhoon Roasters — reviews, sustainability, and specs

Many roasteries evaluating top electric coffee roaster brands for sustainable coffee businesses encounter Typhoon alongside heritage manufacturers.

Typhoon Roasters sustainability & energy performance

Vendor‑provided sustainability claims include:[^typhoon-install][^typhoon-20]

  • Fully electric platform: no gas lines or open flames.

  • Approx. 0.3 kWh/kg energy use across compact and industrial models.

  • Reduced roast defects due to 100% convection fluid‑bed technology.

Typhoon frames this as using roughly 3× less energy per kg than many traditional gas drum roasters; this is a manufacturer comparison based on internal benchmarking and should be treated as indicative rather than a universal standard.

Typhoon Roasters coffee startup equipment: model overview

Selected specs (vendor data):

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO

    • 15 kg/h, 5–7 min roast time, 380–400V, ≈0.3 kWh/kg.[^typhoon-install]

  • Typhoon 5 PRO

    • 30 kg/h, up to 6 batches/hour, 380–400V, ≈0.3 kWh/kg.[^typhoon-install]

  • Typhoon 10 PRO

    • 60 kg/h, up to 6 batches/hour, footprint 2740 × 1600 × 1980 mm, 380–400V.[^typhoon-install]

  • Typhoon 20 kg

    • 100 kg/h, 67 kW connection, 380–400V, back‑to‑back batches with no dedicated cool‑down (vendor claim).[^typhoon-20]

  • Typhoon 30 kg

    • 180 kg/h, 380V, industrial‑scale continuous production.[^typhoon-30]

Typhoon Roasters coffee roaster reviews: where to look

Public third‑party reviews and case studies can be found via:

  • Specialty coffee forums (e.g., r/coffee_roasters discussions comparing Typhoon to Giesen, Probat, Diedrich).[^reddit-typhoon]

  • Customer testimonials and install case studies on Typhoon’s own site.[^typhoon-pitch]

  • Trade show coverage (e.g., World of Coffee showcases) where Typhoon’s fluid‑bed system has been demonstrated.

Pros (based on recurring themes in vendor messaging and user commentary):

  • High throughput relative to footprint

  • Repeatable roast curves via software profiles

  • Lower infrastructure complexity vs gas

Potential cons:

  • Need for adequate 3‑phase electric service and careful planning of demand charges (a point also raised by Diedrich in their analysis of electric roasting costs).[^diedrich-electric]

  • Learning curve for roasters transitioning from traditional drum flavor dynamics.

How Typhoon’s electric platform changes lender & investor conversations

Whether you’re pitching a bank or a private investor, electric fluid‑bed roasting lets you frame the project around throughput, efficiency, and sustainability, not just hardware.

Key talking points for your deck

  1. Clear capacity story

    • Show hourly output (e.g., 30 kg/h for Typhoon 5 PRO, 100 kg/h for Typhoon 20 kg).[^typhoon-install][^typhoon-20]

    • Model revenue per kg roasted and per hour.

  2. Lower and more predictable operating costs

    • Use vendor energy data (0.3 kWh/kg) as a baseline.[^typhoon-install]

    • Compare electric utility rates vs gas costs locally.

  3. Reduced installation risk

    • Reference electric vs gas installation savings (Bellwether’s $15k–$40k estimated range).[^bellwether-cost]

    • Emphasize no gas line dependencies and potentially simpler permitting.

  4. Sustainability and brand value

    • Highlight the move away from fossil fuels and open flames.

    • Show how visible, in‑café roasting can support premium pricing and storytelling.

Typhoon’s own investor guidance stresses the importance of a clear plan with controllability, scalability, and measurable checkpoints (first 90 days, 12 months, and return scenarios).[^typhoon-pitch]

Actionable steps: preparing to finance your roaster

Use this checklist before approaching lenders or lease providers.

  1. Define your production targets

    • Daily and weekly kg.

    • Desired growth over 3–5 years.

  2. Pick a capacity tier and short‑list models

    • Café focus: Typhoon 2.5 PRO or Typhoon 5 PRO.

    • Production focus: Typhoon 10 PRO, Typhoon 20 kg, or Typhoon 30 kg.[^typhoon-install][^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

  3. Estimate total installed cost

    • Equipment MSRP or quote.

    • Electrical, exhaust, construction, permits.

  4. Build a simple ROI and payback model

    • Project roast volumes, margin per kg, and batch throughput.

    • Include tax benefits (e.g., Section 179 in the U.S.).[^irs-946]

  5. Prepare lender‑ready documentation

    • Business plan and financial projections.

    • Equipment spec sheets (Typhoon, Bellwether, etc.).

    • Quotes from installers and contractors.

FAQ: financing electric commercial coffee roasters

Which financing option is best for a small specialty café?

For a single café installing a compact electric roaster, an equipment loan or lease is often the most straightforward.

Equipment loans provide ownership and predictable payments, while leases lower upfront costs and offer flexibility to upgrade.

How do I prepare financials for a lender?

Most banks and SBA lenders will expect:

  • 2–3 years of financial projections

  • A clear explanation of roast volumes and revenue per kg

  • A breakdown of total project cost (equipment + installation)

  • Personal financial statements and collateral details (for small owners)

Including vendor specs (e.g., Typhoon’s capacity and energy data) helps connect the machine’s performance to your revenue model.[^typhoon-install]

Can electric coffee roasters qualify for energy‑efficiency grants?

Yes, in some regions.

In the U.S., rural roasteries may apply under USDA REAP for energy‑efficiency grants if they can demonstrate reduced energy use per unit of output.[^usda-reap]

In other countries, local green‑business or efficiency programs may support similar investments.

Are fully electric commercial coffee roaster reviews positive compared to gas?

Industry commentary increasingly treats electric roasting as a credible alternative.

Manufacturers like PROBAT highlight electric hot‑air systems as flexible and fast‑responding.[^probat-p25e]

User reviews on forums show both enthusiasm and learning‑curve notes, especially for roasters transitioning from traditional drum flavor profiles.[^reddit-typhoon]

How does Typhoon compare to other commercial fluid‑bed coffee roasters for small roasteries?

Typhoon’s key differentiation is high throughput plus low energy use across a scalable platform (2.5 kg to 30 kg), all fully electric.[^typhoon-install][^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

Other brands like Bellwether focus on ultra‑compact shop roasting and integrated cloud profiles.[^bellwether-cost]

The best choice depends on your capacity targets, installation constraints, and desired level of automation.

If you’d like help modeling ROI or choosing the right Typhoon roaster for your café or roastery, Typhoon’s team offers guidance on both equipment selection and business planning.

item.title: From Sample to Production: Adapting Roast Profiles on Typhoon Electric Fluid‑Bed Roasters
item.dc:creator: Typhoon Editorial
item.description: Scaling a beautiful 100 g sample roast into a 10–30 kg production batch is where many roasteries either lock in consistent quality—or start fighting roast…
item.content:encoded:
Scaling a beautiful 100 g sample roast into a 10–30 kg production batch is where many roasteries either lock in consistent quality—or start fighting roast…

Why Sample-to-Production Profiling Matters on Typhoon Roasters

Scaling a beautiful 100 g sample roast into a 10–30 kg production batch is where many roasteries either lock in consistent quality—or start fighting roast defects.

On electric fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon Roasters, you have a different set of tools compared with gas drum roasters: 100% convection, precise airflow, and fully logged automation.

This article explains how to move from sample roasts to full‑scale production on Typhoon equipment without losing cup quality. You’ll get:

  • Practical workflow templates for sample-to-production transfer

  • Data logging practices tailored to Typhoon’s electric, fluid‑bed platform

  • Real‑world examples from Typhoon users

  • Benchmarks for batch size, roast time, and throughput on Typhoon Shop PRO and industrial lines

First Principle: Don’t Copy Curves, Translate Them

Scott Rao, ROEST, and Royal New York all point out the same thing: you should not expect to copy a sample roast curve 1:1 into production.

Even on the same brand of roaster, probes, airflow, and thermodynamics differ. What you can transfer reliably are the sensory targets and the style of heat application.

On Typhoon’s electric fluid‑bed roasters:

  • Sample roasts (50–200 g, usually ~100 g) tell you how much power and development time a coffee prefers

  • Production roasts (2.5–30 kg+) apply that learning through batch size, airflow, and heat application

  • Typhoon’s smart roasting software and logging make those decisions repeatable across operators and days

Think of your sample roast as a sensory blueprint, not a recipe.

Understand Typhoon’s Electric Fluid‑Bed Platform

Before you scale profiles, it helps to frame how Typhoon roasters work.

Typhoon roasters are:

  • Fully electric – no gas lines, open flames, or burners

  • 100% convection / fluid‑bed – beans are suspended in a controlled stream of hot air, not tumbling against a hot drum

  • Fast and efficient – 5–7 minute roast times and around 0.3 kWh per kg on Typhoon 2.5/5/10 PRO models

  • High throughput – up to ~6 batches/hour with no dedicated cool‑down protocol

Typical throughput benchmarks:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO – 2.5 kg nominal batch, ~15 kg/h; matches many 5 kg drum roasters while using about half the energy

  • Typhoon 5 PRO – 5 kg nominal batch, ~30 kg/h; comparable to 10 kg drum output

  • Typhoon 10 PRO – 10 kg nominal batch, ~60 kg/h; comparable to 20 kg drum output

  • Typhoon 20/30 kg industrial – roughly 100–180 kg/h at 5–7 minute roasts

All models share:

  • Transparent roasting chamber (roasting as theatre)

  • Automated loading and exhaust control

  • Smart roasting software with recipe storage and data logging

This common platform is what makes profile transfer easier: once you learn how a coffee behaves on a 2.5 PRO, you’re speaking the same “language” when you move to a 10 or 20 kg Typhoon.

The Four Levers That Protect Cup Quality

On Typhoon’s fluid‑bed roasters, preserving cup quality during scale-up comes down to four main levers:

  1. Batch size

  2. Airflow

  3. Heat application (power curve)

  4. Development time and end temperature

Typhoon’s own defect guide focuses on these when troubleshooting underdevelopment, baking, scorching, tipping, and overdevelopment.

1. Batch Size

Your sample roasts might be 100 g; your production roasts may be 2.5–30 kg.

On fluid‑bed equipment:

  • Stay within the recommended nominal batch range for each Typhoon model

  • Avoid extremely small batches on large machines (e.g., 3–4 kg on a 20 kg roaster) as airflow dynamics change

  • Use batch size adjustments as a tool: slightly reducing batch size can help a delicate, dense washed coffee develop more evenly

2. Airflow

In a fluid‑bed roaster, airflow is not just exhaust—it is the primary heat-transfer mechanism.

To protect cup quality:

  • Ensure beans are properly fluidized (no dead zones or poor circulation)

  • Use higher airflow in drying and Maillard for clean, even heat

  • Consider modest airflow reductions late in the roast if you’re chasing more body—without baking

Typhoon’s automation adjusts airflow for you, but your profiles (recipes) still define how assertive that airflow is over time.

3. Heat Application

Electric elements on Typhoon machines respond quickly, which makes your power curve a powerful creative tool.

For sample-to-production transfer:

  • Use your sample roast to identify power bands: how aggressively you charge, and how you taper before first crack

  • On production batches, reproduce that shape of energy application, not the exact temperature numbers

  • Avoid long, flat energy segments that can lead to baking and dull cups

4. Development Time

Development time and end temperature are usually the most straightforward variables to transfer.

You can usually maintain:

  • Similar development percentage (e.g., 18–22% of total roast time after first crack for a bright but sweet filter roast)

  • Similar end temperature relative to first crack (e.g., 8–12°C above first crack for a medium profile)

On Typhoon, typical total roast times sit in the 5–7 minute range, so development windows are shorter in absolute time but highly controllable.

A Practical Workflow: Sample to Production on Typhoon

Here’s a step‑by‑step workflow combining insights from Scott Rao, ROEST, Royal New York, Artisan, Cropster, and Typhoon’s own training.

Step 1: Run and Cup Your Sample Roasts

Start with multiple small batches, usually around 100 g each.

For each sample roast:

  • Record basic roast data (time to first crack, end time, approximate development percentage)

  • Cup blind and write a plain‑language sensory target, such as:

    • “Preserve lime acidity and florals; avoid drying finish”

    • “Increase sweetness and body; keep citrus but soften edges”

The goal is to define the flavor destination, not lock yourself into one curve.

Step 2: Log Green Coffee Context

This is the metadata that makes your decisions repeatable.

Use Typhoon’s logging plus Artisan/Cropster (if you pair them) to record:

  • Lot ID and origin

  • Process (washed, natural, honey, etc.)

  • Moisture and density (if measured)

  • Screen size

  • Intended use (espresso, filter, omni roast)

These fields become your comparison baseline when you revisit the coffee or move it to a larger Typhoon model later.

Step 3: Define a Production Target, Not a Match

Translate the sensory target into production goals.

Examples:

  • “Same acidity as Sample #3, but +5–10% more development for sweetness and texture”

  • “Match Sample #2’s clarity and absence of defects; slightly lower end temperature for brighter filter profile”

Then express these in Typhoon‑specific operational terms:

  • Batch size (e.g., 2.5 kg on a Typhoon 2.5 PRO)

  • Target roast time (e.g., 6:00–6:30 minutes)

  • Development percentage (e.g., 20%)

  • Energy shape (aggressive early, controlled taper into crack)

Step 4: Run Two Trial Production Roasts

Royal New York suggests at least two trial production roasts after your sample phase. On a Typhoon Shop PRO, that might look like:

Trial Roast A: Bright, sample‑leaning

  • Batch: 2.5 kg

  • Total time: ~5:45

  • First crack: ~4:45

  • Development: 20% (~1:00)

  • End temperature: ~9–10°C above first crack

Trial Roast B: Sweeter, slightly deeper

  • Batch: 2.5 kg

  • Total time: ~6:15

  • First crack: ~4:45

  • Development: 25% (~1:30)

  • End temperature: ~11–12°C above first crack

Cup both roasts against your best sample:

  • If Trial A tastes closest but slightly thin, you can lengthen development by 5–10 seconds

  • If Trial B is sweet but losing top notes, shorten development or reduce energy in late Maillard

Step 5: Lock and Log Your Production Profile

Once you choose a target production roast:

  • Save it as a named Typhoon recipe with all parameters

  • Assign lot ID and customer usage (e.g., “House Espresso – Summer 2026”)

  • Note intended brewing methods and extraction ranges that tasted best

Repeat successful roasts using Typhoon’s automation and your logging stack.

Artisan and Cropster both emphasize that metadata is king: you’re not just storing curves, you’re storing context that makes curves meaningful.

Step 6: Scale to Larger Typhoon Models

When you move from a Typhoon 2.5 PRO to a Typhoon 5 or 10 PRO, you’re still on the same electric fluid‑bed platform.

Best practices for scaling:

  • Keep the roast style constant:

    • Similar total roast time band (5–7 minutes)

    • Similar development percentage

    • Similar energy shape (early push, tapered into crack)

  • Adjust batch size proportionally to the new nominal batch

  • Monitor the first 3–5 batches closely for:

    • Changes in time to first crack

    • Any signs of scorching or tipping

    • Shifts in perceived acidity or body

Typhoon’s industrial roasters (20–30 kg) are built for no‑cooldown, back‑to‑back operation, so once you’ve tuned your profile, you can repeat it at 100–180 kg/h without BBT complexity.

What to Log: A Typhoon Roast Curve Logging Template

Whether you use Typhoon’s native interface alone or pair it with Artisan/Cropster, a structured logging template simplifies profile transfer.

Here’s a practical logging checklist.

Green Coffee Data

  • Lot ID

  • Origin and region

  • Process method

  • Moisture (%), density (g/L)

  • Screen size

  • Intended product (espresso, filter, omni)

Batch and Machine Data

  • Machine model (2.5, 5, 10, 20, or 30 kg Typhoon)

  • Batch size (kg)

  • Batch number (if part of a series)

  • Ambient temperature and humidity

Roast Profile Data

  • Charge temperature

  • Charge time stamp

  • Turning point time

  • Time to color change / yellow

  • Time to first crack

  • End (drop) time

  • End temperature

  • Development time and percentage

  • Airflow settings or profile markers

  • Power application segments (high/medium/low ranges)

Post‑Roast Quality Data

  • Weight loss (%)

  • Color reading (Agtron or similar, if you use it)

  • Cupping notes (structured descriptors and scores)

  • Brew method(s) used for evaluation

This structure mirrors what Artisan Plus and Cropster support, and it maps cleanly onto Typhoon’s automated logging and recipe software.

Real‑World Use: How Typhoon Users Preserve Quality at Scale

Typhoon’s client roster includes specialty roasteries and café chains in Europe, North America, the Philippines, Qatar, and beyond.

From public case pages and training stories, a few themes emerge:

  • Clarity‑first profiles – Many Typhoon users lean toward light and omni‑roast profiles, especially for washed coffees, to showcase origin character

  • Espresso/filter flexibility – Shops often develop a single base profile, then make small development tweaks for espresso vs filter production

  • Back‑to‑back consistency – With up to 6 batches/hour and no between batch protocol, roasteries can run continuous production while keeping roast curves tight

A typical Typhoon workflow in a multi‑café operation might look like:

  1. Sample roast and cup new arrivals on a small electric roaster

  2. Develop a core profile on a Typhoon 2.5 or 5 PRO in the flagship café

  3. Log and freeze that profile as a Typhoon recipe with full metadata

  4. Replicate the same recipe on a 10 or 20 kg Typhoon in the production roastery

  5. Deliver defect‑free, consistent coffee to multiple locations with minimal retraining

Because all Typhoon roasters share the same fluid‑bed logic, baristas and production teams talk in the same terms about roast style and curve behavior.

Electric vs Gas: Why Typhoon Simplifies Profile Transfer

Scaling profiles on Typhoon Roasters is usually more straightforward than on gas drum roasters because:

  • Heat is pure convection, not a mix of conduction, convection, and radiation

  • Electric elements respond predictably; you’re not juggling gas pressure, burner tuning, and drum speed

  • Beans see even heat across the entire mass, reducing hot spots and contact scorching

From a profiling perspective, that means:

  • Less concern about localized defects when you change batch size

  • More focus on the overall energy budget and airflow pattern

  • Cleaner cup quality at higher throughput

Many roasteries view Typhoon as both a quality upgrade and an efficiency/sustainability play:

  • Around 0.3 kWh/kg energy use on PRO models (roughly 3× less energy per kg than many traditional setups)

  • No gas infrastructure, easier permitting, and lower operating costs

Actionable Checklist: Maintaining Cup Quality When You Scale

Use this quick checklist whenever you move from sample to production on a Typhoon electric fluid‑bed roaster.

Before Production:

  • [ ] Cup at least 3 sample roasts blind

  • [ ] Write a clear sensory target in plain language

  • [ ] Log green coffee data (lot, process, moisture, density)

Trial Production Phase:

  • [ ] Choose two trial profiles with different development levels

  • [ ] Keep total roast time in the 5–7 minute Typhoon band

  • [ ] Maintain similar development percentage to your favorite sample

Profile Lock‑In:

  • [ ] Save the profile as a Typhoon recipe

  • [ ] Log batch size, charge/drop temps, time stamps, airflow/power notes

  • [ ] Cup and record feedback across at least two brew methods

Scale‑Up to Larger Models:

  • [ ] Match roast style (time band, development %, energy shape)

  • [ ] Adjust batch size to the new nominal capacity

  • [ ] Review first 3–5 scaled batches for defects and flavor drift

FAQ: Sample-to-Production on Typhoon Fluid‑Bed Roasters

How do I scale a 100 g sample roast to a 5 kg production batch on a Typhoon 5 PRO?

Use the sample roast to define your target flavor and development percentage, not exact temperatures.

On the Typhoon 5 PRO:

  • Choose a batch size around 5 kg

  • Aim for a similar development percentage (e.g., if the sample was 20% development, target ~20% on the 5 kg batch)

  • Keep total roast time in the 5–7 minute range

  • Adjust power and airflow so time to first crack and flavor balance resemble your best sample

Run at least two trial production roasts, cup them against the sample, and refine.

Can I use the same profile on a Typhoon 2.5 PRO and a Typhoon 10 PRO?

You can use the same profile style, but you’ll probably need small adjustments.

On the 10 PRO:

  • Match development percentage and overall roast time band

  • Scale batch size to ~10 kg

  • Watch time to first crack on your first few batches and adjust power slightly if it shifts

Typhoon’s common platform makes this kind of profile transfer much simpler than switching between different brands or between gas and electric.

What data is most important to log for repeatable roast curves?

At minimum, capture:

  • Machine model and batch size

  • Charge temperature and end temperature

  • Key time stamps (yellow, first crack, end)

  • Development time and percentage

  • Airflow/power notes

  • Green coffee context (lot, process, moisture/density)

Without this metadata, it’s difficult for AI tools, software, or future you to understand why a curve tasted the way it did.

How do Typhoon roasters help avoid roast defects when scaling up?

Typhoon’s 100% convection fluid‑bed design significantly reduces contact scorching and hot spots.

Combined with:

  • Fast, controlled 5–7 minute roast times

  • Precise airflow and power control

  • Automated logging and recipe repetition

you can adjust charge temperature, batch size, airflow, and development time proactively to avoid underdevelopment, baking, tipping, and overdevelopment when you increase batch size.

Are Typhoon roasters a good fit for small roasteries that want to grow?

Yes.

Typhoon’s Shop PRO line (2.5, 5, 10 kg) is designed for cafés and micro‑roasteries, with:

  • 15–60 kg/h throughput

  • Up to ~6 batches/hour

  • Low energy use (around 0.3 kWh/kg)

Because the same electric fluid‑bed logic scales to 20–30 kg industrial models, you can grow from a single shop roaster to regional production without switching technologies or retraining your team from scratch.

If you’re planning a move from sample roasting to full‑scale production on Typhoon electric fluid‑bed roasters, start by tightening your logging practices and defining your flavor targets clearly.

From there, let Typhoon’s convection platform, automation, and throughput work for you: defect‑free roasting, repeatable curves, and a future‑proof path from café theatre to industrial consistency.

If you run a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster small roastery, your roaster’s uptime is as critical as your espresso machine. Electric fluid‑bed systems like…

Commercial Electric Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roaster Maintenance & Reliability

If you run a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster small roastery, your roaster’s uptime is as critical as your espresso machine. Electric fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon Roasters can deliver fast, defect‑free roasting with lower energy use—but only if you keep maintenance structured, predictable, and simple.

This guide outlines a practical electric coffee roaster maintenance checklist for fluid‑bed roasters, with cleaning routines, inspection points, spare‑parts planning, and uptime metrics. We reference Typhoon’s own service standards and industry benchmarks so you can build a reliability strategy that scales with your production.

Note: All Typhoon‑specific data is based on manufacturer claims and published support materials.[^typhoon10][^typhoonservice]

Electric Coffee Roaster Maintenance Checklist (Fluid‑Bed Roasters)

Fluid‑bed roasters depend on clean, unrestricted airflow, accurate sensors, and reliable electrical components. That makes housekeeping and preventive checks more important than periodic gas‑burner tuning.

Industry checklists from Cropster and OEMs show a clear cadence emerging: light cleaning every few hours, deeper cleaning weekly and monthly, and a structured annual review.[^cropster]

Daily / Every Shift (6–8 Hours of Operation)

Focus: airflow hygiene, chaff control, and visible safety.

  • Wipe down roaster exterior and nearby surfaces every 6–8 hours to prevent oil/dust buildup.[^cropster]

  • Empty chaff collector regularly:

    • Cropster: every 2 hours or 10 roasts.[^cropster]

    • Typhoon guidance: every 8–10 roasts or before the bucket is half full.[^typhoonclean]

    • Sonofresco warns that failing to clean chaff after each roast can cause a fire and progressively darker roasts due to restricted airflow.[^sonofresco]

  • Visually check transparent roasting chamber (where applicable) for unusual smoke, residue, or uneven bean agitation.

  • Confirm cooling tray is clear of bean fragments, chaff, and debris.

  • Listen for abnormal fan or motor sounds—grinding, squealing, or rattling can signal bearings or motor issues.

For a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small scale roastery, these daily steps are often handled by baristas or production techs between batches.

Weekly Tasks (Every 3–5 Days of Heavy Use)

Focus: deeper cleaning and early wear detection.

Many roastery checklists recommend the following every 3–5 days of production.[^cropster]

  • Vacuum under cooling tray and interior compartments:

    • Use a dry vacuum with at least 15–20 kPa suction and fine‑dust filtration to handle chaff and coffee particles.

  • Clean ducts and accessible airflow paths to remove lint and chaff buildup.

  • Blow out motors and fans:

    • Use dry compressed air at moderate pressure (e.g., 4–6 bar) to clear dust without damaging bearings.

  • Lubricate moving parts (where manufacturer recommends), such as mechanical linkages or door hinges.

  • Inspect bolts, brackets, and fasteners for looseness or vibration marks.

  • Check cable strain reliefs and connectors for visible wear, discoloration, or heat damage.

Typhoon’s maintenance philosophy emphasizes keeping a written log for these tasks and recording any unusual observations before they become failures.[^typhoonclean]

Monthly Tasks (Every 4 Weeks)

Focus: roaster‑level cleaning and sensor accuracy.

Cropster’s reference checklist suggests a monthly deep clean and component review for commercial roasters.[^cropster]

  • Degrease roaster surfaces and accessible interior panels:

    • Use non‑corrosive, electronics‑safe degreasers (e.g., isopropyl alcohol 70–90% on metal surfaces away from plastics; manufacturer‑approved food‑grade cleaners elsewhere).

    • Avoid strong alkaline or acidic cleaners near sensors, wiring, and control panels.

  • Clean fans, ducts, and chaff collector walls to maintain optimal airflow.

  • Clean cooling tray screens and bins so beans cool consistently.

  • Replace or clean air filters according to OEM guidance.

  • Check thermocouples and temperature sensors:

    • For most specialty roasters, Type K thermocouples are standard.

    • Aim for calibration within ±1–2 °C across the typical roast curve range (say 150–230 °C).

    • If readings drift more than 3–5 °C from reference instruments or known profile behavior, plan a replacement.

Typhoon roasters use multiple thermocouples to control fully electric, 100% convection roasting, so sensor accuracy is a key part of repeatability.[^typhoon10]

Annual Tasks (Or Every 2000–2500 Roast Cycles)

Focus: uptime, safety, and long‑term reliability.

Industry guidance recommends a full roastery deep clean and safety review at least once per year.[^cropster][^loring]

  • Full deep clean of roaster and exhaust path:

    • Remove panels as allowed by OEM guidelines.

    • Vacuum and wipe all accessible interior surfaces.

  • Check all thermocouples and wiring harnesses for insulation cracks, corrosion, or loose terminals.

  • Inspect control electronics:

    • Solid State Relays (SSRs) typically rated 25–40 A at appliance voltage.

    • Contactors suitable for the roaster’s heater load (often 3‑phase, 20–60 A depending on size).

    • Inspect for discoloration, cracked casings, or heat damage.

  • Test safety systems (emergency stop, over‑temperature cut‑outs, door interlocks).

  • Retrain staff on the preventative maintenance schedule for coffee roaster equipment and update logs.

OEMs like Diedrich and Coffee Crafters increasingly productize this annual care via toolkits and critical spare parts kits.[^diedrich][^coffeecrafters]

Fluid‑Bed Roaster Cleaning Procedure & Preventative Maintenance Schedule

A fluid‑bed roaster relies on a high‑velocity stream of hot air to suspend and heat the beans evenly. Any restriction in that airflow—especially chaff buildup—directly impacts roast quality and safety.

Core Fluid‑Bed Roaster Cleaning Procedure

A simple, repeatable cleaning procedure keeps your roaster at peak without consuming your entire day.

  1. Power down and cool the machine before any internal cleaning.

  2. Empty chaff collector:

    • After each batch or every few batches, depending on OEM guidance.

    • Never let chaff exceed half the collector’s volume for safety and consistent airflow.[^typhoonclean]

  3. Vacuum roasting chamber surroundings:

    • Use a non‑conductive nozzle; avoid direct contact with sensors.

  4. Clean cooling tray and screens:

    • Brush off loose chaff and residue.

    • Vacuum underneath cooling tray as needed.

  5. Wipe interior viewing windows:

    • Soft cloth and OEM‑approved cleaner to maintain visibility for profile monitoring.

  6. Inspect fan intakes and grills for lint, dust, or obstructions.

Sonofresco’s documentation highlights the risk: failing to clean chaff collector after each roast can cause fires and progressively darker roasts from restricted airflow.[^sonofresco]

Recommended Preventative Maintenance Schedule

You can combine industry benchmarks with Typhoon’s own maintenance philosophy to build a schedule tailored to your throughput.

A practical starting point for a busy small roastery:

  • Light cleaning: every shift (6–8 hours).

  • Chaff collector empty: every 2 hours or 8–10 roasts.

  • Weekly inspection and cleaning: 3–5 days of operation.

  • Monthly deep clean and sensor check: every 4 weeks.

  • Annual safety and reliability review.

Typhoon encourages keeping a written log split into daily/weekly/monthly/yearly entries, plus notes on odd sounds or unexpected cup results, to catch issues early.[^typhoonclean]

Spare Parts Strategy for Commercial Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roasters

Even the best electric commercial coffee roaster will experience wear on electrical components over time. Planning a spare‑parts list keeps you ahead of failures and protects your uptime.

Core Roaster Spare Parts List

OEMs like Coffee Crafters sell “critical spare parts” kits covering the components most likely to fail in everyday service.[^coffeecrafters]

Typical spares for fluid‑bed roasters include:

  • Solid State Relays (SSRs)

    • Current rating: often 25–40 A at mains voltage.

    • Keep at least one spare per major heater circuit.

  • Contactors

    • Sized for heater and blower motor loads (commonly 3‑phase, 20–60 A).

  • Heater elements

    • OEM‑specific wattage; having one replacement set for primary elements can prevent multi‑day downtime.

  • Thermocouples and temperature probes

    • Extra Type K probes and thermocouple wire for bean and exhaust sensors.

  • Blower motors and capacitors

    • For key fans delivering fluid‑bed airflow.

  • Switches and potentiometers

    • Rocker switches and control knobs used frequently.

  • Fuses and breakers

    • OEM‑specified ratings for fast replacement.

Coffee Crafters’ kits include combinations of SSRs, contactors, motor brushes, thermocouple wire/probes, rocker switches, potentiometers, fuses, and heating elements.[^coffeecrafters]

Typhoon roasters use high‑quality European components and are tested against a 48‑point checklist before shipment, but a structured spare‑parts inventory still safeguards production.[^typhoon10]

In‑House vs OEM‑Managed Maintenance

  • In‑house:

    • Daily and weekly cleaning.

    • Visual inspections, basic electrical component replacement (SSRs, switches, thermocouples) when trained.

  • OEM‑managed:

    • Complex electrical troubleshooting.

    • Software or automation issues.

    • Structural repairs or major mechanical replacements.

Typhoon supports operators with remote troubleshooting, spare parts dispatch, and on‑site technicians when needed.[^typhoonservice]

Typhoon Roasters: Service Standards & Reliability Claims

Typhoon positions its fully electric convection platform as a high‑throughput, low‑downtime alternative to traditional gas drum roasters.[^typhoon10][^typhoonservice]

Typhoon 10 PRO Example (Manufacturer Claims)

The Typhoon 10 PRO is a mid‑scale commercial fluid‑bed roaster designed for growing roasteries.[^typhoon10]

Key manufacturer‑stated data:

  • Capacity: 10 kg nominal batch size.

  • Throughput: up to 6 batches/hour, about 60 kg/h continuous production with no between‑batch cool‑down protocol.

  • Energy use: around 0.3 kWh per kg roasted.

  • Quality control: 48 quality tests before shipment.

All of these figures are Typhoon OEM claims based on their published product information.[^typhoon10]

Typhoon Support & Service Model (Manufacturer Claims)

Typhoon’s service program is designed to minimize downtime rather than just sell hardware.[^typhoonservice]

Published support standards include:

  • Two‑year warranty on roasters.

  • Remote troubleshooting as the first support step.

  • Spare parts shipment when remote diagnosis identifies component failure.

  • On‑site technician within 5–10 business days if remote help doesn’t resolve the issue.

  • Complimentary roastmaster training course during installation and calibration.

  • Around 50+ professionals per year graduating from the Typhoon Roastmaster program.[^typhoonservice]

Typhoon emphasizes that every roaster meets CE standards and uses high‑quality European components.[^typhoonservice]

Regional note: service response times, installation requirements, and exhaust/vent permits vary by country and city. Always confirm local regulations and Typhoon’s region‑specific service commitments when planning your roastery.

Uptime Metrics for Commercial Coffee Roaster Reliability

Reliability is no longer a vague feeling; it’s an operational KPI. Concepts like Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and availability help you quantify how well your roasting line is performing.

Definitions You Can Use

  • Availability: uptime ÷ (uptime + downtime).

    • NASA illustrates this with simple math and examples.[^nasa]

  • MTBF: average time a repairable asset operates before failing.[^ibm]

A food manufacturing case study focused on a specialty coffee roasting facility showed that predictive analytics lifted equipment uptime to 97% and cut unplanned downtime by 81%.[^ifactory]

At different availability levels, monthly downtime looks like this for a 30‑day month:[^nasa]

  • 97% availability ≈ 21.6 hours downtime/month.

  • 99% availability ≈ 7.2 hours downtime/month.

  • 99.5% availability ≈ 3.6 hours downtime/month.

  • 99.9% availability ≈ 0.72 hours downtime/month.

For a roastery running 8–10 hours per day, gaining back 15–20 hours of uptime each month can easily justify investment in maintenance routines, spare‑parts kits, and better monitoring.

Actionable Steps for Growing Roasteries Using Electric Fluid‑Bed Roasters

If you’re scaling from a café‑level Typhoon Shop PRO to a 10–30 kg industrial roaster, a consistent maintenance playbook keeps your flavor and reliability aligned.

Practical steps:

  1. Document your electric coffee roaster maintenance checklist clearly.

  2. Build a spare‑parts shelf with SSRs, probes, switches, and a heater set.

  3. Train staff on daily/weekly cleaning and basic sensor checks.

  4. Track uptime and downtime per month so you can spot trends.

  5. Set escalation rules: what your team fixes vs when you call Typhoon or your OEM.

Typhoon’s combination of electric fluid‑bed technology, transparent chambers, automation, and structured service makes it a strong candidate for reliability‑focused roasteries that want both speed and consistency.[^typhoon10][^typhoonservice]

FAQ: Electric Fluid‑Bed Roaster Maintenance & Typhoon Reliability

Q1. How often should I perform a preventative maintenance schedule for a coffee roaster?

You should follow a layered schedule:

  • Every shift (6–8 hours): wipe surfaces, check airflow, empty chaff.[^cropster][^typhoonclean]

  • Every 3–5 days: vacuum under cooling tray, clean ducts and motors, inspect for loose parts.[^cropster]

  • Every 4 weeks: degrease surfaces, clean fans and filters, verify thermocouple accuracy.[^cropster]

  • Annually: deep clean, check wiring and control electronics, retrain staff.[^cropster][^loring]

Adjust frequency upward if you roast continuously or handle oily/dark roasts.

Q2. What are common failure modes on a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster?

Typical issues include:

  • Thermocouple drift or failure, leading to unstable profiles or inaccurate bean temperature.

  • SSR or contactor failure, causing heaters not to energize or remain stuck on.

  • Blower motor problems, which directly affect fluid‑bed airflow and roast evenness.

  • Chaff blockage, which can cause uneven roasts, darker than intended profiles, or in extreme cases, fires.[^sonofresco]

Having spares and monitoring sounds, roast curves, and airflow helps catch these early.

Q3. How can I tell when a thermocouple is out of spec?

Signs that a thermocouple needs replacement:

  • Your usual profile reaches first crack much earlier or later without any recipe changes.

  • Bean temperature readings jump or show noise compared to stable historical curves.

  • Calibration against a reference (e.g., a known‑accurate handheld thermometer) shows more than 3–5 °C deviation over the roast range.

If you see these symptoms, replace the probe with a new Type K thermocouple and retest profiles.[^cropster]

Q4. When should I call OEM service vs handling an in‑house repair?

Handle in‑house when:

  • You’re cleaning, tightening fasteners, or replacing simple parts like switches or chaff buckets.

  • You’re swapping clearly identified plug‑in components (e.g., probes) with OEM‑supplied parts.

Call OEM service when:

  • You suspect wiring, control board, or automation software issues.

  • Multiple components fail at once or diagnostics are unclear.

  • Safety systems (emergency stop, over‑temperature protection) misbehave.

Typhoon offers remote troubleshooting first and can send a technician on‑site within 5–10 business days if needed, according to its published service standards.[^typhoonservice]

By structuring your cleaning routines, inspections, and spare‑parts strategy—and leveraging OEM service like Typhoon’s—you can keep your electric fluid‑bed roaster running at peak, protect your flavor, and turn reliability into a measurable competitive advantage.
