How electric fluid‑bed engineering turns airflow into cleaner, faster, more consistent coffee roasting.

Inside Typhoon Roasters’ Patented Fluid‑Bed Convection Technology

How electric fluid‑bed engineering turns airflow into cleaner, faster, more consistent coffee roasting.

Meta title & description

Meta title: Typhoon Roasters patented fluid‑bed convection technology explained | Electric commercial coffee roaster

Meta description: Discover how Typhoon Roasters’ patented fluid‑bed convection technology uses controlled airflow and 100% electric heat to deliver uniform, defect‑free coffee roasting with up to 6 batches/hour and ~0.3 kWh/kg energy use.

What makes Typhoon’s fluid‑bed roaster different?

Typhoon Roasters builds fully electric, 100% convection commercial coffee roasters that use a patented fluid‑bed technology to levitate and heat beans in a controlled stream of hot air.[^typhoon-about][^patent]

Instead of a hot metal drum, high‑velocity air enters from below, suspends the beans, and transfers heat almost entirely by convection.[^patent][^bh-airflow]

The result is:

  • Very uniform bean temperatures

  • Reduced scorching and tipping

  • Faster roast cycles (around 5–7 minutes in many production setups)[^typhoon-10][^typhoon-20]

  • Repeatable, software‑driven roast curves

Typhoon moved all models to fully electric, 100% air roasting in 2023, positioning the platform as a gas‑free alternative for modern specialty roasteries.[^sprudge]

Key idea: 100% convection, 0% drum contact. Heat comes from moving air, not a glowing steel surface.

How the patented fluid‑bed technology works

1. Airflow generation and control

Typhoon’s core design follows classic fluidized‑bed physics: a blower pushes hot air upward through a perforated plate beneath the beans.[^patent]

As air velocity increases, beans transition from resting on the plate to “fluidized,” where they behave like a boiling liquid.

In the Typhoon roaster:

  • An electric heater raises inlet air to the target temperature.

  • A high‑pressure blower delivers that air into the roasting chamber from below.

  • Automated dampers and exhaust adjust airflow and pressure in real time.[^typhoon-about]

  • Software monitors temperature and airflow and follows a stored roast profile.

Patent documentation describes beans being “levitated” in the air stream, with chaff drawn off via the exhaust path and separated before cooling.[^patent]

This design means airflow is the main control knob for heat transfer and defect prevention, aligning with independent explanations from Barista Hustle and other educators that emphasize airflow as the critical driver of convection in roasting systems.[^bh-airflow]

2. Heat transfer by convection, not conduction

In a drum roaster, beans contact a hot metal surface; heat moves via conduction (contact) and radiation. If the drum wall overheats, you can get surface scorching, tipping, and uneven internal development.[^rao-imf]

In Typhoon’s fluid‑bed roaster:

  • Convection dominates: Hot air surrounds each bean and transfers heat evenly across its surface.

  • Minimal conduction: There is little direct contact with hot metal, so no localized hot spots.

  • Stable inlet temperature: You can run higher air temperatures without overheating a drum, because there is no drum.[^rao-imf]

Scott Rao notes that air roasters transfer heat almost entirely by convection and can roast faster than drum machines precisely because they avoid overheated drum surfaces that sear bean exteriors.[^rao-imf]

3. Bean movement and mixing

Uniform roast development requires every bean to experience similar temperature history.

In a fluid‑bed roaster, bean movement is created by air, not by paddles or vanes.

Typhoon’s patent describes:

  • Beans suspended in an upward air stream.

  • Continuous circulation as beans rise and fall in the chamber.

  • Chaff removal through the same airflow path.[^patent]

Academic work on small batch fluidized‑bed roasters confirms that at the right air velocity, beans mix intensely and achieve very high uniformity.

A 2021 study on a small fluidized‑bed prototype (batch size not specified, but designed as a batch lab roaster) found:[^bsu]

  • Optimal air velocity around 9.2 m/s

  • Roasting efficiency of 94.06% for medium roast and 96.46% for dark

  • Roast uniformity of 99.80% (medium) and 99.97% (dark)

  • Roast times of 13.68 minutes (medium) and 17.98 minutes (dark)

These figures were measured using Arabica beans, with roast degree quantified via color and moisture analysis. While that prototype roasted slower than Typhoon’s production machines, the study illustrates how properly tuned airflow can deliver almost perfectly uniform beans.

From engineering to cup: why convection matters

1. Uniformity: fewer hot spots, cleaner flavor

Typhoon’s design aims to minimize internal heat gradients in the bean mass.

Because beans float in a moving air stream:

  • Each bean sees similar convective heat transfer.

  • There is less temperature difference between beans at the top and bottom of the batch.

  • There is reduced risk of localized over‑roasting near a hot surface.[^patent][^bh-airflow]

Independent fluidized‑roaster research backs this up, showing near‑perfect roast uniformity when airflow is optimized.[^bsu]

In the cup, this translates to:

  • Cleaner flavor separation

  • Lower incidence of baked or underdeveloped notes

  • More consistent color and solubility between batches

Barista Hustle links baked coffee to crashes in rate of rise around first crack and emphasizes that consistent energy application is key to avoiding such defects.[^bh-defects] Fluid‑bed convection helps maintain stable heat delivery, supporting smoother roast curves.

2. Speed: 5–7 minute roast cycles and 6 batches/hour

Typhoon’s production roasters are engineered for shorter cycle times than many traditional drum systems, largely because convection can deliver heat faster without scorching.[^rao-imf]

Manufacturer‑stated figures (which should be treated as Typhoon’s own claims, not independent lab results) include:[^typhoon-2-5][^typhoon-5][^typhoon-10][^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

  • 2.5 PRO

    • Capacity: up to 15 kg/h

    • Roast time: typically 5–7 minutes

    • Up to 6 batches/hour

    • Energy use: around 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Claimed to match the output of a 5 kg drum roaster

  • 5 PRO

    • Capacity: up to 30 kg/h

    • Up to 6 batches/hour

    • Output comparable to a 10 kg drum roaster

  • 10 PRO

    • Capacity: around 60 kg/h

    • Roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Up to 6 batches/hour

    • Energy use: around 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Claimed output similar to a 20 kg drum roaster

  • 20 kg industrial

    • Capacity: 100 kg/h, up to 120 kg/h depending on configuration

    • Roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Around 6 batches/hour

    • Energy use: around 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Claimed hourly output comparable to a 40 kg drum roaster

  • 30 kg industrial

    • Capacity: around 180 kg/h

    • Roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Around 6 batches/hour

    • Energy use: around 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Claimed similar hourly capacity to larger drum systems

These cycle times are based on Typhoon’s internal testing and customer case studies. Real‑world performance will vary with batch size, roast degree, and ambient conditions.

How ‘batches/hour’ is defined here:

  • A batch refers to a full load at the machine’s nominal batch mass (e.g., 2.5 kg for the 2.5 PRO, 10 kg for the 10 PRO).[^ ]

  • Batches/hour is calculated as the number of full batches a roaster can produce in one hour, including loading, roasting, discharge, and cooling, under continuous production.

  • Typhoon emphasizes that no dedicated cool‑down cycle is required between batches; the roaster is designed to avoid heat buildup between roasts.[^typhoon-about]

3. Energy efficiency and how kWh/kg is measured

Typhoon reports energy usage of approximately 0.3 kWh per kg of roasted coffee across its electric lineup.[^typhoon-10][^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

These numbers are manufacturer claims and, according to Typhoon’s documentation, are:

  • Based on standard production roasts to medium profiles

  • Calculated as total electrical energy consumed (heaters + blowers + controls) divided by roasted bean mass

  • Measured without separate gas afterburners, since the roaster is fully electric

The company positions this as using “about 3× less energy per kg” than many traditional gas setups.[^typhoon-10][^typhoon-20] That comparative statement depends heavily on the baseline:

  • Typical gas drum reference: Many gas drum roasters with external afterburners can reach combined energy intensities around 0.9–1.0 kWh/kg equivalent when burner efficiency, stack losses, and afterburner fuel are included, as reported in efficiency case studies from manufacturers like Loring and others.[^loring-efficiency]

  • Typhoon baseline: Around 0.3 kWh/kg in their own tests.[^typhoon-10]

Because methods differ, any comparison should be treated as approximate and context‑specific. For rigorous benchmarking, roasteries should log their own energy use with submeters.

4. Defect reduction: less scorching and tipping

Roast defects like scorching, tipping, and baked flavors are closely tied to how energy is delivered over time.

  • Loring’s technical paper on roasting defects notes that excessive surface heat, especially early in the roast, can cause tipping and scorching, while unstable energy input later can lead to baked profiles.[^loring-defects]

  • Barista Hustle emphasizes that excessive conduction and uneven airflow contribute directly to such issues.[^bh-airflow][^bh-defects]

Typhoon’s fluid‑bed approach addresses those factors by:

  • Minimizing direct contact with hot metal surfaces

  • Maintaining high, stable airflow to remove smoke and chaff

  • Using software‑controlled profiles to avoid rate‑of‑rise crashes

Scott Rao’s commentary on air roasters supports this: because heat transfer is almost entirely convection, roasters can run higher air temperatures without overheating a drum surface, reducing the risk of surface defects while still achieving full internal development.[^rao-imf]

In practice, many Typhoon users report fewer visual defects on the bean surface and cleaner cups, especially when pushing faster profiles.

Electric roaster vs gas drum roaster

Key differences in everyday use

When roastery owners compare an electric fluid‑bed roaster to a gas drum roaster, they typically evaluate four areas: installation, control, energy, and flavor.

Installation and infrastructure

  • Electric fluid‑bed (Typhoon):

    • No gas lines or burners

    • Simplified permitting in many regions

    • No external afterburner required (though you still need proper ventilation)[^typhoon-about]

  • Gas drum:

    • Requires gas supply, regulators, and regular safety inspections

    • Often needs an afterburner or catalytic converter to meet emissions rules

Control & automation

  • Fluid‑bed roasters rely on airflow and inlet temperature as primary control variables.

  • Modern platforms like Typhoon store roast recipes, automate fan and heater control, and repeat curves across operators.[^typhoon-about]

  • Many drum roasters now also offer profile automation, but must manage both drum temperature and airflow.

Energy & sustainability

  • Electric convection simplifies energy accounting because all energy is electrical.

  • Gas systems may have lower immediate energy prices in some markets, but total efficiency depends on burner tuning, stack losses, and afterburner use.[^loring-efficiency]

  • For brands emphasizing decarbonization or all‑electric builds, electric roasting aligns with broader sustainability goals.

Flavor profile

  • Fluid‑bed roasting is often described as producing clean, transparent cups with high clarity and low roastiness.

  • Drum roasting can emphasize body and caramelization, especially with longer development.

  • In practice, profile design matters more than machine category; both systems can produce a wide range of styles.

Typhoon Roasters coffee roaster reviews and user feedback

Typhoon reports more than 1,000+ roasters installed worldwide with only about 6% service calls over 15 years, according to its 30 kg industrial model page.[^typhoon-30] These numbers are self‑reported manufacturer data rather than audited statistics.

Common themes in user testimonials and third‑party discussions (e.g., trade show feedback, specialty forums) include:

  • Consistency: Operators note that saved profiles and automation help new staff reproduce roasts with minimal deviation.

  • Speed: Roasteries transitioning from traditional drums often highlight increased throughput, especially when moving from ~3–4 batches/hour to ~6 batches/hour at similar capacity.[^typhoon-10]

  • Clean cup profile: Some users describe Typhoon roasts as “cleaner” or “more transparent,” especially for lighter specialty profiles.

  • Learning curve: Roasters with a drum background mention that fluid‑bed behavior (especially rate of rise) takes some adaptation.

For an objective picture, prospective buyers should:

  • Request references from Typhoon and speak directly with existing customers.

  • Ask for sample roast curves and cupping feedback from similar green coffee types.

  • Where possible, run A/B tests between current equipment and a Typhoon test roast.

Best electric commercial coffee roaster: why choose a fluid‑bed roaster?

If you search for “best electric commercial coffee roaster,” you’ll encounter a mix of small tabletop units and a few industrial‑scale electric platforms. Typhoon’s fluid‑bed roasters are designed to fill the gap between compact plug‑in devices and large gas machines.

Key reasons roasteries consider fluid‑bed electric roasters:

  • Scalable capacity: From 2.5 kg shop roasters up to 30 kg industrial roasters, all built on the same convection platform.[^typhoon-2-5][^typhoon-30]

  • Repeatable roast curves: Software control and automated airflow give consistent results across operators.[^typhoon-about]

  • Compact footprint: No gas train or external afterburner reduces space requirements.

  • Sustainability narrative: Fully electric roasting aligns with renewable energy sourcing and corporate ESG goals.

  • In‑store experience: Transparent chambers and low emissions make roasting a visual centerpiece inside cafés.[^typhoon-about]

For many specialty businesses, the “best” electric roaster is the one that balances quality, speed, energy, and brand story. Fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon are engineered to hit all four.

FAQ: Typhoon’s patented fluid‑bed convection technology

What is Typhoon Roasters’ fluid‑bed patent about?

Typhoon’s U.S. patent (US10765137B1) covers a coffee roasting apparatus where beans are levitated in a hot air stream, with specific designs for airflow, chaff separation, and cooling.[^patent]

The patent details:

  • A perforated plate and chamber shape that promote stable fluidization

  • Integrated chaff removal via exhaust

  • A separate cooling stage with controlled airflow

This protects Typhoon’s particular implementation of fluid‑bed roasting rather than the general concept, which has existed in various forms for decades.

How does Typhoon control airflow and heat during a roast?

Typhoon uses electric heaters, variable‑speed blowers, and automated dampers to control airflow and temperature.[^typhoon-about]

The control technology:

  • Measures temperature at multiple points in the chamber

  • Adjusts fan speed and heater power to follow a predefined profile

  • Stores recipes so operators can repeat roast curves with minimal manual intervention

Airflow is the primary lever, especially for modulating heat transfer and smoke removal.

How are energy use and batches/hour measured on Typhoon roasters?

According to Typhoon’s spec sheets:[^typhoon-10][^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

  • kWh/kg is calculated as total electrical consumption during roasting (heaters + blowers + controls) divided by the mass of roasted coffee produced.

  • Measurements are based on typical medium roasts to production batch sizes, under standard ambient conditions.

  • Batches/hour is the number of nominal‑size batches completed in one hour of continuous production, including load, roast, discharge, and cooling.

These metrics are manufacturer‑reported; roasteries can (and should) validate them with their own energy monitoring and throughput tracking.

Does fluid‑bed roasting always produce better coffee than drum roasting?

Not automatically.

Fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon provide very even convective heat transfer and can reduce certain defects, but flavor depends heavily on profile design, green quality, and operator skill.

Both fluid‑bed and drum roasters can:

  • Produce exceptional coffee when well‑operated

  • Develop a wide range of roast styles, from light to dark

The main advantages of fluid‑bed are speed, uniformity, and repeatability; how you translate that into flavor is up to your roasting strategy.

Is Typhoon Roasters a good fit for small cafés and micro‑roasteries?

Typhoon specifically targets:

  • Specialty cafés that want to roast in‑house with 2.5–5 kg machines

  • Growing roasteries needing 10–30 kg roasters with 60–180 kg/h capacity[^typhoon-2-5][^typhoon-5][^typhoon-10][^typhoon-20][^typhoon-30]

Because all models share the same fluid‑bed convection platform and software, cafés can grow into larger machines without retraining from scratch.

Cafés should consider:

  • Electrical capacity on site

  • Desired throughput (kg/h)

  • In‑store aesthetic and customer experience goals

If you’d like help modeling capacity, energy use, or ROI for a Typhoon setup in your roastery, Typhoon offers consultation and online resources tailored to both startup roasteries and established production teams.

item.content:encoded:
Selecting a compact commercial coffee roaster for a small café in an urban building is no longer just about fitting a drum into a corner. It’s about balancing…

Selecting a compact commercial coffee roaster for a small café in an urban building is no longer just about fitting a drum into a corner. It’s about balancing production, energy use, ventilation, and permitting — while keeping roasting at the heart of your brand.

This guide walks café owners through how to choose the best electric commercial coffee roaster for a specialty café, using Typhoon’s compact fluid‑bed roasters as a practical blueprint.

Commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small scale roastery

For a small roastery or café‑roastery hybrid, three questions come first:

  1. How much coffee do you actually need to roast per hour?

  2. How much floor space and ceiling height do you truly have?

  3. What does your local regulator require for roasting and exhaust systems?

Electric, fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon Shop PRO 2.5 and 5 are designed to answer all three. They deliver meaningful throughput in footprints that actually fit inside urban cafés.

Electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roastery startup

If you’re starting a roastery in a dense city, the choice between electric and gas often decides whether your project is feasible at all. Here’s the practical comparison for a roastery startup:

Gas drum roaster (typical scenario)

  • Needs gas lines, shut‑off valves, and burner permitting

  • Often requires high‑temperature exhaust plus separate afterburner

  • Longer roast + cool‑down cycles (commonly 3–4 batches/hour)

  • Higher and more volatile energy costs (gas prices, flue losses)

Electric fluid‑bed roaster (Typhoon‑style scenario)

  • No gas infrastructure; powered via 3‑phase electricity only

  • 100% convection: beans are suspended in hot air, not pressed against hot metal Typhoon fluid‑bed blog

  • Up to 6 batches/hour without dedicated cool‑down on compact models Typhoon 2.5 PRO, Typhoon 5 PRO

  • Typical energy use around 0.3 kWh per kg roasted, based on Typhoon’s internal electrical measurements across their PRO line Typhoon 2.5 PRO specs

Typhoon positions this 0.3 kWh/kg figure as roughly 2–4× less energy than many gas drum setups at similar capacity. To understand the comparison:

  • 1 kWh ≈ 3,412 BTU

  • A traditional 5–10 kg gas drum roaster often uses burners in the 60,000–120,000 BTU/hr range (manufacturer specs; e.g., many classic drum roasters list burner ratings in this band)

  • If that drum roaster produces ~15–30 kg/h, simple division yields roughly 2,000–4,000 BTU/kg, or 0.6–1.2 kWh/kg

  • Against Typhoon’s stated 0.3 kWh/kg, that’s approximately 2–4× more energy per kg on gas

Actual numbers will vary by model and setup, but the method above shows how kWh/kg vs BTU/hr figures are converted and compared. For exact energy audits, café owners should request per‑model consumption data from each manufacturer.

Typhoon small roaster models — specs and use cases

Typhoon’s compact shop roasters are designed specifically as electric coffee roasters for urban cafés. Below are the key facts café owners and architects need.

Typhoon 2.5 PRO — compact commercial coffee roaster for small café

According to the official Typhoon 2.5 PRO datasheet Typhoon 2.5 PRO:

  • Batch size & throughput

    • Nominal batch: 2.5 kg of green coffee

    • Throughput: up to 15 kg/hour

    • Cadence: up to 6 batches/hour (no dedicated cool‑down)

  • Dimensions & footprint

    • Size (L × W × H): 1800 × 1150 × 1650 mm

    • Footprint: ~2.07 m²

    • As a practical rule of thumb, plan for an installation area of ~6 m² to allow for operator movement, hopper access, exhaust routing, and service clearances

  • Electrical requirements

    • Supply: 3‑phase, typically in the 380–400V range (regional variants may exist; confirm with Typhoon’s electrical data sheet)

    • Connection power: internal spec indicates peak draw sized for 2.5 kg fluid‑bed roasting at 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Café owners should design for:

      • Breaker size and amperage as specified in the machine’s CE electrical plate

      • Dedicated circuit with neutral and protective ground per local electrical code

      • Allowance for inrush current at startup, as stated in Typhoon’s electrical documentation

  • Energy efficiency claim

    • Typhoon quotes 0.3 kWh/kg based on its internal load measurements under typical production roasting Typhoon 2.5 PRO specs

  • Certification & support

    • CE‑certified equipment

    • 2‑year warranty

    • Complimentary roastmaster training course at installation

    • Remote support with technician visits typically within 5–10 business days if needed Typhoon Service

Use case fit:

  • Ideal for cafés roasting 10–15 kg/day on‑site

  • Great for small roasteries with limited floor area who want roasting as part of the customer journey

Typhoon 5 PRO — best commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small roastery scaling up

For cafés or micro‑roasteries needing more output without leaving the city core, the Typhoon 5 PRO offers double the hourly capacity in a modestly larger footprint. Official datasheet: Typhoon 5 PRO.

  • Batch size & throughput

    • Nominal batch: 5 kg

    • Throughput: up to 30 kg/hour

    • Cadence: up to 6 batches/hour

  • Dimensions & footprint

    • Size (L × W × H): 2150 × 1300 × 1900 mm

    • Footprint: ~2.80 m²

    • Typhoon notes that the 5 PRO delivers roughly the same hourly output as a 10 kg drum roaster at much lower energy use Typhoon 5 PRO

  • Electrical requirements

    • Voltage: 380–400V, 3‑phase

    • Connection power: sized to support up to 30 kg/h at 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Planners should request the exact:

      • Rated current (A)

      • Recommended breaker size

      • Plug / connector type and wiring (L1–L2–L3–N–PE) from Typhoon’s comprehensive electrical diagram before submitting to building engineers

  • Energy efficiency claim

    • Same 0.3 kWh/kg benchmark as the 2.5 PRO, based on Typhoon’s internal power logging Typhoon 5 PRO specs

Use case fit:

  • Designed for small roasteries producing 20–40 kg/day or regional operations needing 30 kg/h in tight urban footprints

  • Strong option when you want a compact commercial coffee roaster for small café plus wholesale in one machine

Compact competitor benchmarks (for context)

To position Typhoon against other top electric coffee roasters for sustainable businesses, consider these commonly researched alternatives:

  • Bellwether Shop Roaster Bellwether:

    • Batch: 1.5 kg

    • Throughput: 3–4 roasts/hour (≈4.5–6 kg/h)

    • Voltage: 220V single‑phase

    • Footprint: less than 4.5 sq ft counter space

    • Ventless system with built‑in filtration; marketed heavily to cafés and hotels

  • Coffee‑Tech Solar Eco Coffee‑Tech:

    • Batch: 2 kg, fully electric and automatic

    • Designed for compact shop roasting

  • Giesen W1E Giesen:

    • Batch: 0.75–1.5 kg

    • Throughput: up to 7.5 kg/hour

    • W1 series includes gas burner options; the W1E is the electric variant

  • PROBAT BRZ Sample Roaster Probat:

    • Batch: 80–100 g per drum, 2‑ or 4‑drum configuration

    • Electric, but intended for sampling, not café production

Bellwether®, Coffee‑Tech®, Giesen®, and PROBAT® are trademarks of their respective owners. Typhoon Roasters is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by any of these companies.

Below is a quick comparison focused on café‑scale production.

Compact roaster layout for tight spaces — blueprint essentials

When planning a compact commercial coffee roaster for a small café, layout matters as much as specs. Here’s how to think about your floorplan.

Minimum space and clearances

As a practical rule of thumb, its shop roasters can be installed in as little as 6 m² of floor area. Within that envelope, plan for:

  • Machine footprint

    • 2.5 PRO: ~2.07 m²

    • 5 PRO: ~2.80 m²

  • Operator working zone

    • At least 800–1000 mm in front of the roaster for safe operation and bean discharge

    • Side clearance (~600 mm) for access to panels and duct connections

  • Service access

    • Rear and side access per Typhoon’s installation guide (obtain from Typhoon’s service team)

    • Height clearance above the hopper and exhaust connection (allow ≥300–500 mm above the stated machine height for ductwork)

  • Weight & floor loading

    • Exact machine weights are provided on Typhoon’s shipping documents and technical sheets; urban cafés should:

      • Confirm floor load rating (kN/m²) with their structural engineer

      • Verify that staircases, lifts, and doorways can handle the roaster weight and crate dimensions

    • When in doubt, request shipping weight, unpacked weight, and crate dimensions from Typhoon before finalizing logistics

Example urban installation scenarios

Typhoon lists a variety of compact café‑roastery installs which show what is possible in dense settings Typhoon Clients:

  • Current Coffee Roasters, Cebu City — café‑roastery in a busy urban environment

  • Puck Provisions, Singapore — roasting inside a city café with visible equipment as part of the experience

  • Roastery 29, Sibiu — small European roastery in a compact footprint

  • Campus Cafe showroom, Paris — demonstration and training roaster in a tight city space

  • Expe Coffee, Lausanne/Prilly — café‑roastery hybrid in a dense Swiss urban zone

These installations demonstrate that a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small scale roastery can fit in high‑rent spaces, provided layout and ventilation are carefully planned.

Commercial coffee roaster ventilation requirements in urban buildings

Even with electric roasting, most cities treat coffee roasting as a process that needs controlled exhaust. Understanding the basics will help you design a compliant, future‑proof system.

Typical ventilation metrics planners should know

While exact numbers must come from your mechanical engineer and local code, café owners planning an electric coffee roaster instead of gas roaster should be ready to discuss:

  • Exhaust airflow (CFM / m³/h)

    • Many small roasters use exhaust fans in the 500–1500 CFM range (approx. 850–2550 m³/h), depending on batch size and after‑treatment equipment

    • Typhoon’s specific CFM requirement is listed in its installation manual; request this before MEP design

  • Duct diameter & materials

    • Common diameters for café‑scale roasters: 150–250 mm round duct

    • Materials: galvanized steel or stainless steel, rated for the exhaust temperature and any condensate

  • Run limits & offsets

    • Keep horizontal runs as short as practical; many mechanical codes advise a preference for vertical discharge

    • Limit the number of elbows; each bend adds resistance that must be factored into fan sizing

    • Maintain required clearance from windows, doors, and air intakes per local mechanical code (often ≥3 m horizontal, or as specified)

  • Filtration & treatment

    • Depending on local regulations, expect one or more of:

      • Cyclone for chaff and particulate

      • HEPA or multi‑stage filters for particulates and odor

      • Electrostatic or catalytic systems where ventless or near‑ventless operation is needed

Typhoon’s roasters typically use cyclones and ducted exhaust; the exact configuration depends on model and local requirements. The mechanical drawings supplied by Typhoon include connection sizes and recommended layouts.

Regulatory examples — know your district’s rules

To frame the permitting landscape, Typhoon often references how agencies classify roasting equipment. For example, South Coast Air Quality Management District (South Coast AQMD) in California publishes specific thresholds for coffee roasting operations AQMD Coffee Roasting:

  • The advisory describes permit needs based on:

    • Roaster type (drum vs floating‑bed / fluid‑bed)

    • Batch capacity (lb)

    • Combined heat input (BTU/hr)

  • As of the referenced advisory:

    • Drum‑type roasters with cyclone generally require permits when batch capacity > 18 lb (~8.2 kg) or combined heat input ≥ 1 million BTU/hr

    • Floating‑bed roasters with cyclone (i.e., fluid‑bed) often trigger permits at batch capacity > 12 lb (~5.4 kg) or combined heat input ≥ 1 million BTU/hr

    • Natural‑gas afterburners at ≥ 1 million BTU/hr need a separate Authority to Construct

Important caveats:

  • These thresholds are examples only, specific to the South Coast AQMD advisory; they are not universal rules for all cities

  • Other regions may have different limits or classify electric roasters differently

  • Always check your local air quality district, building department, and fire authority for up‑to‑date requirements

Additionally, the International Mechanical Code (IMC) treats the exhaust from coffee roasting under ventilation rules in Chapter 5, typically requiring independent exhaust systems for process equipment. Your mechanical engineer should reference the latest IMC and local amendments when designing your system.

Best electric commercial coffee roaster for specialty café — decision checklist

To select the best commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for a small roastery or café, use this practical checklist.

1. Production requirements

  • Daily roasted coffee volume (kg/day)

  • Peak hourly needs (kg/h) during busiest days

  • Future growth (e.g., wholesale or additional cafés)

For most single cafés:

  • 10–15 kg/day → Typhoon 2.5 PRO is usually sufficient

  • 20–40+ kg/day → Typhoon 5 PRO offers more headroom

2. Space and layout

  • Confirm clear floor area (≥6 m² recommended around the roaster)

  • Measure ceiling height to allow for ducting above the machine height

  • Map customer flow so roasting becomes a feature, not a bottleneck

3. Electrical infrastructure

  • Confirm available 3‑phase 380–400V supply or its local equivalent

  • Obtain Typhoon’s electrical data sheet for:

    • Maximum current (A)

    • Recommended breaker size

    • Required wiring (phases, neutral, earth)

  • Verify panel capacity with a licensed electrician

4. Ventilation and permitting

  • Request Typhoon’s installation drawings for exhaust connection and minimum CFM

  • Engage a mechanical engineer to size ducts (diameter, length, fan) to local code

  • Check with:

    • Local air quality district (for roasting permits)

    • Building department (for exhaust and mechanical systems)

    • Fire authority (for process safety and clearances)

5. Support, warranty, and training

  • Typhoon offers:

    • 2‑year warranty

    • CE certification on equipment

    • Complimentary roastmaster training during startup

    • Remote support and on‑site technicians within 5–10 business days when needed Typhoon Service

This reduces risk compared with buying purely on specs. You’re getting an equipment platform plus a partner in launching your roastery.

Action steps — bring compact electric roasting into your café

If you’re ready to explore an electric coffee roaster for an urban café rather than a traditional gas drum, here’s a concise roadmap:

  1. Define your production profile

    • Write down daily and peak hourly roast needs

    • Decide if you will expand into wholesale in the next 2–3 years

  2. Measure and sketch your space

    • Capture floor area, ceiling height, and nearby walls/openings

    • Draw a simple compact roaster layout for tight spaces showing the machine, operator zone, and duct path

  3. Collect infrastructure data

    • Request Typhoon’s 2.5 PRO and 5 PRO spec sheets and installation manuals

    • Share electrical and exhaust requirements with your engineer

  4. Check regulatory constraints early

    • Call your local air quality agency and building department

    • Reference example frameworks like South Coast AQMD but confirm local rules

  5. Talk to Typhoon’s team

    • Ask for Typhoon coffee roaster installation examples similar to your building type

    • Review ROI, energy use, and capacity modeling based on 0.3 kWh/kg and your local electricity rate

By following these steps, you can confidently choose a compact commercial coffee roaster for a small café that fits your space, stays compliant, and elevates your brand.

FAQ — compact electric roasters for small cafés

How much space does a compact commercial coffee roaster for a small café need?

Typhoon’s shop roasters are designed to install in roughly 6 m² of space. The 2.5 PRO footprint is ~2.07 m², and the 5 PRO footprint is ~2.80 m², with the remaining area reserved for operator movement, service access, and ducting. Always confirm exact clearances using Typhoon’s installation drawings and your architect’s plan.

Do electric coffee roasters require special ventilation in urban buildings?

Yes. Even fully electric systems generate warm, odorous exhaust that typically needs dedicated ducting, fans, and filtration. Typhoon’s roasters use cyclones and exhaust connections specified in the installation manual; planners must size CFM, duct diameter, and discharge location per local mechanical code and air‑quality rules.

Are Typhoon Roasters more energy efficient than gas drum roasters?

Typhoon reports ~0.3 kWh/kg electrical consumption on its PRO line, based on internal measurements. Many gas drum roasters at similar capacities use burners rated in the 60,000–120,000 BTU/hr range, which often equates to roughly 0.6–1.2 kWh/kg when converted using 1 kWh ≈ 3,412 BTU. That suggests Typhoon’s electric fluid‑bed approach can use about 2–4× less energy per kg, but café owners should request exact energy data from each manufacturer to confirm.

What electrical infrastructure do I need for a Typhoon 2.5 or 5 PRO?

Both models use 3‑phase 380–400V power. You will need a dedicated circuit, properly sized breaker, neutral and protective earth, and allowance for startup current as specified on the roaster’s CE electrical plate and wiring diagram. Typhoon provides detailed electrical documentation; share it with your electrician and engineer before installation.

Where can I see real‑world Typhoon coffee roaster reviews and installations?

Typhoon publishes client stories and installation photos from cafés and roasteries worldwide, including urban sites in Cebu City, Singapore, Paris, Sibiu, and Lausanne/Prilly. These examples show how compact electric fluid‑bed roasters integrate into small cafés and tight urban spaces; you can browse them on Typhoon’s official client page.

item.title: How to Scale a Roastery from 15 to 100 kg/h | Best Electric Commercial Coffee Roaster Guide (Typhoon Roasters)
item.dc:creator: Typhoon Editorial
item.description: Electric roasting has moved from niche to mainstream. For growing roasteries, it’s now a serious path to higher throughput, lower energy use, and more…
item.content:encoded:
Electric roasting has moved from niche to mainstream. For growing roasteries, it’s now a serious path to higher throughput, lower energy use, and more…

Meta description: Learn how to scale a roastery from 15 kg/h to 100 kg/h using the best electric commercial coffee roaster setup, including batch size strategy, scheduling, and automation.

How to Scale a Roastery from 15 to 100 kg/h

Electric roasting has moved from niche to mainstream. For growing roasteries, it’s now a serious path to higher throughput, lower energy use, and more predictable production.

This guide walks through how to scale a roastery from 15 kg/h to 100 kg/h using electric commercial coffee roasters, with a focus on Typhoon Roasters’ fluid‑bed platform.

We’ll cover:

  • Electric coffee roaster capacity (kg per hour) and what the numbers really mean

  • Batch size strategy from café scale to industrial output

  • Scheduling and throughput planning for roasteries

  • Roast automation systems and workflow continuity

  • A worked ROI example and what “stepped capacity growth” looks like in practice

TL;DR: Key Takeaways for Scaling Electric Throughput

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO: ~15 kg/h

  • Typhoon 5 PRO: ~30 kg/h

  • Typhoon 10 PRO: ~60 kg/h

  • Typhoon 20 kg: ~100 kg/h

All are fully electric, fluid‑bed commercial roasters with 5–7 minute roast times and up to ~6 batches/hour when operators run near full capacity.

These models make it practical to move from 15 to 100 kg/h in steps, instead of jumping directly from a small shop roaster to a large industrial roaster.

Electric Coffee Roaster Capacity (kg per hour): How to Read the Numbers

When you compare electric coffee roaster capacity (kg per hour), it’s important to understand the assumptions behind each figure.

Typhoon Roasters capacity ladder

According to Typhoon’s published specifications (Typhoon Roasters):

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO

    • Nominal batch: 2.5 kg

    • Throughput: 15 kg/h

    • Typical roast time: 5–7 minutes per batch

    • Electrical: 23A, 380–400V

  • Typhoon 5 PRO

    • Nominal batch: 5 kg

    • Throughput: 30 kg/h

    • Typical roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Electrical: 38A, 380–400V

  • Typhoon 10 PRO

    • Nominal batch: 10 kg

    • Throughput: 60 kg/h

    • Typical roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Electrical: 69A, 380–400V

    • Includes automatic loading, airflow and exhaust control (Typhoon Roasters)

  • Typhoon 20 kg

    • Nominal batch: 20 kg

    • Throughput: 100 kg/h

    • Typical roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Electrical: 98A, 380–400V

    • Fully automatic control for continuous production (Typhoon Roasters)

  • Typhoon 30 kg

    • Nominal batch: 30 kg

    • Throughput: 180 kg/h

    • Typical roast time: 5–7 minutes

    • Electrical: 210A, 380–400V (Typhoon Roasters)

What “up to 6 batches/hour” actually assumes

Typhoon’s stated 15–180 kg/h capacities assume roughly:

  • 5–7 minutes roast time per batch

  • Minimal idle time between batches

  • Fast loading and post‑roast handling

  • An operator working with prepared greens and labels

In practice, your real‑world throughput depends on:

  • Bean type (dense washed coffees vs naturals)

  • Desired roast level (light vs dark)

  • Cooling and bagging speed

  • Staffing and scheduling discipline

Typhoon’s fluid‑bed convection technology allows roasting and cooling to happen in parallel, so there is no separate dedicated cool‑down cycle between batches. Cooling still takes time, but it doesn’t block the roasting chamber from starting the next batch.

Why Electric Fluid‑Bed Roasters Scale Differently

Convection‑driven roasting (with caveats)

Typhoon’s platform is built around patented fluid‑bed convection technology, using a controlled stream of hot air to heat the bean mass evenly.

  • Heat transfer is primarily convective, with much less direct contact heating than in classic gas drum roasters.

  • This reduces common defects like scorching and tipping and helps keep internal gradients lower (Typhoon Roasters).

“100% convection” in marketing terms means the primary heat delivery is via hot air, but in any real roaster there are minor conductive and radiative effects. Operationally, you can think of Typhoon as a fluid‑bed roaster that behaves like a controlled hot‑air oven, not a gas‑heated rotating drum.

Energy efficiency and electrification

Typhoon reports an energy use of ~0.3 kWh per kg of roasted coffee on its fully electric roasters (Typhoon Roasters).

Many traditional gas drum setups, when you include burner efficiency and ancillary fans, often land around 0.9 kWh/kg or equivalent energy input. That’s why Typhoon positions its roasters as using roughly 3× less energy per kg than many conventional systems.

Exact comparisons depend on:

  • Local gas and electricity prices

  • Burner tuning and maintenance

  • Ventilation and afterburner use

But if your electricity is competitively priced—or increasingly renewable—electric fluid‑bed roasting can be both a cost and sustainability advantage.

Stepped Capacity Growth: A Roadmap from 15 to 100 kg/h

One of the biggest risks in roastery expansion is over‑investing in capacity too early. Typhoon’s product line is unusually “stepwise” for electric roasting, making it easier to grow in logical increments.

Step 1: 15 kg/h — Early‑stage roastery or café roaster

Best fit:

  • Single café roasting in‑house

  • Micro‑roastery doing up to 100–150 kg/week

Typical setup:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO

  • 2–3 production days per week

  • 4–5 batches per production day (light schedule)

This is a safe starting point if you’re validating your brand, dialing in profiles, and building local wholesale volume.

Step 2: 30 kg/h — Growing local roastery

Once you consistently hit 150–300 kg/week, a move to 30 kg/h often makes sense.

Typical setup:

  • Typhoon 5 PRO

  • 2–3 production days per week

  • 6–10 batches per day

You now have room for:

  • More SKUs (decaf, seasonal lots)

  • Better batching (full 5 kg loads)

  • A buffer for wholesale growth without weekend overflow roasting

Step 3: 60 kg/h — Regional roastery entering multi‑location distribution

When you reach 300–700 kg/week, bottlenecks tend to show up in:

  • Between‑batch workflows

  • Cooling and packaging

  • Staff fatigue

This is where a Typhoon 10 PRO (60 kg/h) with automatic loading and exhaust control becomes meaningful. At this tier, a single 8‑hour shift can roast about 480 kg of coffee if you maintain near full utilization (60 kg/h × 8 h = 480 kg) (Typhoon Roasters).

Step 4: 100 kg/h — Established regional roastery

At 700–1,500+ kg/week, you’re in true production territory. A Typhoon 20 kg (100 kg/h) can roast around 800 kg per 8‑hour shift at full utilization (100 kg/h × 8 h = 800 kg) (Typhoon Roasters).

This is appropriate when:

  • You supply multiple café locations or supermarket chains

  • You run at least 3–4 production days per week

  • You have staff dedicated to production, packaging, and QC

Thanks to shared UI and profile logic across Typhoon models, your operators don’t have to relearn a new roasting language as you move up the ladder.

Batch Size Strategy for Commercial Coffee Roasting

Why batch size matters

Batch size is your primary lever for balancing:

  • Roast consistency

  • SKU flexibility

  • Production throughput

For commercial fluid‑bed coffee roasters like Typhoon, ideal batch sizes are generally 70–100% of nominal capacity. Batching too small can:

  • Waste energy

  • Introduce more variability in bean lofting and heat transfer

Practical batch size strategy at each tier

  • On a 2.5 PRO (15 kg/h)

    • Target 2.0–2.5 kg batches

    • Use smaller batches only for R&D or ultra‑limited lots

  • On a 5 PRO (30 kg/h)

    • Target 4–5 kg batches

    • Keep standard blends at full 5 kg to simplify scheduling

  • On a 10 PRO (60 kg/h)

    • Target 8–10 kg batches

    • Use automation for consistent loading weights

  • On a 20 kg (100 kg/h)

    • Target 16–20 kg batches

    • Align batch size with packaging formats (e.g., multiples of your most common bag size)

Integrating batch size with product mix

To keep a sane workflow:

  • Group roasts by process and roast level (e.g., all washed espresso roasts together)

  • Avoid constant batch size changes within a production block

  • Use your reference profiles as anchors and plan batch sizes around them

Cropster’s scheduling guidance, for example, explicitly focuses on the number of batches needed and optimal batch size per order set (Cropster).

Scheduling and Throughput Planning for Roasteries

From ad‑hoc roasting to demand‑led production

Moving from ad‑hoc roasting to order‑led scheduling is one of the biggest performance gains for any roastery.

Cropster reports that a 750 kg/week roastery recovered ~20 hours per month after shifting from manual planning to demand‑led scheduling tied to orders and inventory (Cropster).

Core scheduling questions to answer

For each production week:

  1. How many kg must we roast?

  2. Which SKUs, and in what batch size?

  3. Which roaster is best for each SKU?

  4. How many batches does that represent per roaster?

  5. What is the ideal sequence to minimize changeovers and downtime?

Typical scheduling pattern at different capacities

  • At 15–30 kg/h

    • 1–2 roast days/week

    • 6–12 batches/day

    • Manual scheduling in spreadsheets or simple software

  • At 60 kg/h

    • 2–4 roast days/week

    • 20–30 batches/week

    • Order‑driven schedules using tools like Cropster or Giesen Profiler

  • At 100 kg/h

    • 3–5 roast days/week

    • 40–60+ batches/week

    • Dedicated production planning, batch grouping, and between‑batch protocols

Cropster’s Between Batch Protocol suggests many roasteries can move from 2–3 to 3–4 batches/hour just by tightening between‑batch workflows (Cropster). Typhoon’s fast fluid‑bed roaster and no‑cooldown requirement make those gains even more accessible.

Roast Automation Systems for Commercial Roasters

What “automation” means in practice

Electric commercial roasters now commonly include:

  • Profile storage and replay (time, temperature, airflow curves)

  • Automatic loading and discharge

  • Airflow and exhaust control

  • Integration with planning software (e.g., Cropster, Artisan)

Typhoon’s 10 PRO, 20 kg and 30 kg models add automatic loading and fully automatic roasting control, turning recipes into consistent, repeatable batches while still allowing manual override (Typhoon Roasters).

Why automation matters when scaling

Automation supports scaling by:

  • Reducing operator variability

  • Lowering training time for new staff

  • Making it easier to replicate profiles across multiple roasters

PROBAT, Giesen, Coffee‑Tech and Typhoon all lean on profile transfer and electric/hybrid heating to keep flavour profiles consistent when you upgrade equipment (PROBAT, Giesen, Coffee‑Tech).

Sample ROI & Payback Scenario (with Assumptions)

Typhoon often speaks about fast ROI for growing roasteries. Instead of broad claims, here’s a simple example you can adapt.

Assumptions table

Let’s compare moving from 15 kg/h (Typhoon 2.5 PRO) to 60 kg/h (Typhoon 10 PRO).

Capacity & utilization

  • 2.5 PRO capacity: 15 kg/h

  • 10 PRO capacity: 60 kg/h

  • Utilization rate (production): 60% of max

  • Production days/month: 16 days

  • Hours/day on roaster: 6 hours

Economics

  • Green coffee margin: €3 per kg roasted (net contribution after COGS)

  • Electricity cost: €0.20 per kWh

  • Typhoon energy use: 0.3 kWh/kg (Typhoon Roasters)

  • Labor cost: €20 per hour (loaded)

Equipment cost (illustrative only)

  • 2.5 PRO sunk cost

  • 10 PRO capital cost: €45,000 (example, actual pricing varies by region and options)

Throughput comparison

At 60% utilization:

  • 2.5 PRO

    • 15 kg/h × 6 h/day × 16 days = 1,440 kg/month

  • 10 PRO

    • 60 kg/h × 6 h/day × 16 days = 5,760 kg/month

Incremental monthly capacity gain:

  • 5,760 kg − 1,440 kg = 4,320 kg/month additional potential

Profit and payback approximation

Incremental profit from extra capacity, if you can sell it:

  • 4,320 kg × €3/kg margin = €12,960/month gross contribution

Incremental energy cost:

  • 4,320 kg × 0.3 kWh/kg = 1,296 kWh/month

  • 1,296 kWh × €0.20/kWh = €259/month

Labor impact will depend on your staffing model. If you’re already running a roaster for those hours, the main change is more output per paid hour.

Simple payback period:

  • Equipment: €45,000

  • Net incremental margin ≈ €12,960 − €259 ≈ €12,700/month

  • Payback ≈ €45,000 ÷ €12,700 ≈ 3.5 months

This example assumes:

  • You can actually sell the extra volume

  • Existing space and permitting can support the larger roaster

  • Other bottlenecks (packaging, storage) are addressed

Your real ROI will vary with:

  • Local energy prices

  • Actual equipment cost

  • Sales velocity

  • Labor structure

Use this as a template, not a forecast.

Typhoon Roasters vs Loring Smart Roast: Sustainability Context

Many roasteries compare Typhoon Roasters vs Loring Smart Roast when evaluating sustainability. While detailed spec‑by‑spec comparison is beyond this article, here’s the high‑level context.

  • Fuel type

    • Typhoon: fully electric fluid‑bed roasters

    • Loring: gas‑fired drum/convection systems with integrated burners

  • Energy narrative

    • Typhoon: ~0.3 kWh/kg electric use and claims of ~3× less energy per kg than many gas drum roasters (Typhoon Roasters)

    • Loring: focus on high gas efficiency and integrated roasting/afterburner to lower gas use per kg compared with traditional drum setups

  • Decarbonization options

    • Typhoon: can run on renewable electricity contracts or on‑site solar

    • Loring: can benefit from lower‑carbon gas sources but still relies on combustion

In short, Typhoon’s sustainability story is tied to electrification and low kWh/kg, while Loring’s is tied to high gas efficiency and integrated emissions control.

Loring®, PROBAT®, Giesen®, and Diedrich® are trademarks of their respective owners. Typhoon Roasters is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by any of these companies.

Electric Coffee Roaster vs Gas Drum for Roastery Startups

For startups comparing electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roastery startup options, the decision often comes down to infrastructure and flexibility.

Electric advantages

  • No gas line installation or burner tuning

  • Easier siting in mixed‑use buildings (subject to local code)

  • Simpler multi‑site replication (same electrical spec, similar controls)

Drum/gas advantages

  • Broadly familiar to many roasters

  • Long heritage and a large installed base

If you value:

  • Lower energy per kg

  • No dependence on gas

  • Consistency and faster roast cycles

Electric fluid‑bed platforms like Typhoon, PROBAT’s P‑series electric models, Giesen W6E/W15E, or Coffee‑Tech’s shop roasters are all strong contenders (PROBAT, Giesen, Coffee‑Tech).

Typhoon Roasters Coffee Roaster Reviews & Operator Feedback

Public Typhoon Roasters coffee roaster reviews tend to emphasize:

  • Clean, defect‑free cups

  • Fast roast cycles and back‑to‑back roasting

  • Strong onboarding and support

Typhoon reports installations at 500+ roasteries worldwide and highlights:

  • Online roasting courses

  • Dedicated service managers

  • 2‑year warranties

  • 48‑point inspection and ~20 test roasts per machine before shipment (Typhoon Roasters).

For balanced research, roastery owners typically compare Typhoon with Probat, Giesen, Diedrich, Loring, IMF, and Coffee‑Tech, and read peer feedback on forums like r/coffee_roasters on Reddit (Reddit).

Infographic: Fluid‑Bed Scalability at a Glance

Here’s a quick visual of how Typhoon’s capacity ladder helps you scale without over‑investing.

These incremental steps let you match capital expenditure to real demand instead of leaping straight from café scale to 100+ kg/h.

Permits, Ventilation, and Emissions: What Electric Roasting Does (and Doesn’t) Change

Electric simplifies fuel; it doesn’t erase emissions

Electric roasters remove:

  • Gas lines

  • Burners and open flames

But coffee roasting still produces:

  • Smoke and VOCs

  • Odors

  • Fine particulate matter

The US EPA and NIOSH both note that roasting can require controls such as afterburners or thermal oxidizers in some facilities, depending on volume and location (EPA).

Jurisdictional notes (high level)

Regulations vary widely, but generally:

  • EU

    • Local air‑quality rules may limit roasting emissions in dense urban areas

    • Expect requirements for proper ducting, filtration, and sometimes thermal treatment

  • US & Canada

    • City and state/provincial codes govern ventilation and air permits

    • Larger roasteries may need air permits and formal emission controls

  • Asia & other regions

    • Rules range from minimal to very strict depending on city/region

In all cases, you should:

  • Consult local building and fire codes

  • Check with environmental authorities about VOC and odor rules

  • Plan for adequate ducting, filtration, and possibly catalytic or thermal oxidizers

Electric roasters like Typhoon simplify fuel infrastructure and permitting, but you still need to address air handling and emissions appropriately.

Actionable Next Steps for Growing Roasteries

To move from 15 to 100 kg/h in a sane, profitable way:

  1. Model your demand

    • Current weekly kg

    • 12–24 month growth scenarios

  2. Choose a capacity step

    • 2.5 PRO (15 kg/h) for early validation

    • 5 PRO (30 kg/h) for growing locals

    • 10 PRO (60 kg/h) or 20 kg (100 kg/h) for regional production

  3. Design your batch size strategy

    • Aim for 70–100% of nominal batch size

    • Tie batches to SKUs and packaging formats

  4. Implement order‑led scheduling

    • Use planning tools (Cropster, similar) to tie roasts directly to orders

    • Standardize between‑batch protocols

  5. Leverage automation

    • Use profile storage and replay

    • Automate loading and exhaust where available

  6. Check permits and infrastructure early

    • Electrical supply and panel capacity

    • Ventilation and emission control requirements

Typhoon Roasters can help map your current demand to the right roaster size and future upgrades, keeping your workflow and software consistent as you grow.

FAQ: Scaling Production with Electric Roasters

1. How do I know if I should move from 15 kg/h to 30 kg/h?

If you regularly roast more than 150–300 kg/week, struggle to fit production into 1–2 days, or find yourself roasting on weekends, it’s time to consider moving from a 2.5 PRO (15 kg/h) to a 5 PRO (30 kg/h). Use your past 3–6 months of sales data to project forward and decide.

2. What is the best batch size strategy for a small roastery?

For a small roastery on a 5 kg electric roaster, aim for 4–5 kg batches for core products. Reserve smaller batches for limited lots and R&D. This keeps energy use efficient and simplifies scheduling.

3. Can I run a Typhoon roaster inside my café?

Many Typhoon Shop PRO installations are inside cafés. However, you must comply with local building, fire, and air‑quality regulations, including proper ducting and, if required, odor and VOC control. Electric roasting helps with fuel safety, but emissions rules still apply.

4. Does electric roasting change flavour compared to gas drums?

Electric fluid‑bed roasting typically yields cleaner cups with fewer defects, thanks to more even convection heating. Flavour differences vs gas drums are mostly about heat transfer and profile design, not electricity vs gas per se. Most roasteries can match or improve their target flavour profiles with careful profile development.

5. How do Typhoon Roasters support scaling beyond equipment?

Typhoon offers:

  • Online roasting courses

  • Assistance with choosing the right roaster size

  • Dedicated service managers and 24‑hour response

  • Thorough pre‑shipment testing of each machine

This makes them a partner in building your roastery, not just an equipment supplier (Typhoon Roasters).

If you’d like a capacity and ROI model tailored to your numbers, Typhoon’s team can help map your current and projected volume to the right electric roaster configuration and upgrade path.

item.title: Best Electric Commercial Coffee Roaster: Data‑Driven, Customer‑Facing Roasters for Specialty Cafés
item.dc:creator: Typhoon Editorial
item.description: Electric, data‑driven roasting is shifting from a niche idea to a practical standard for modern specialty cafés and roasteries. At the same time, roasting is…
item.content:encoded:
Electric, data‑driven roasting is shifting from a niche idea to a practical standard for modern specialty cafés and roasteries. At the same time, roasting is…

Best Electric Commercial Coffee Roaster for Specialty Cafés

Electric, data‑driven roasting is shifting from a niche idea to a practical standard for modern specialty cafés and roasteries. At the same time, roasting is moving out of back rooms and into customer‑facing spaces.

In this article, we’ll explore where commercial coffee roasting is headed—electric heat, sensor‑rich control, and visible roaster design—and how Typhoon Roasters’ platform helps you prepare for that future.

We’ll also compare leading brands, outline trade‑offs, and give you a practical checklist for choosing the best electric commercial coffee roaster for your specialty café.

The Future of Commercial Coffee Roasting: Electric, Data‑Driven, Visible

Three major shifts are defining the next decade of commercial roasting:

  • Electrification of roasting equipment

  • Data‑driven, sensor‑rich control systems

  • Customer‑facing roaster design inside cafés and showrooms

These aren’t abstract trends; they’re already visible in new products, regulations, and café concepts.

1. Electrification: From Niche to Portfolio Standard

Electric commercial roasters have moved beyond 1–2 kg tabletop units and into serious production machines. Daily Coffee News’ 2024 coverage of the SCA Expo noted that new professional roasting equipment leaned heavily into electronics, automation, and repeatable push‑button operation, including electric‑heat machines in the 1–15 kg range.[^1]

In December 2024, PROBAT announced its P25e, stating that the launch completed the electrification of its specialty roaster portfolio.[^2] This is a strong signal: when a heritage manufacturer electrifies an entire specialty line, electric heat is no longer fringe.

At the same time, fully electric systems like Bellwether’s plug‑in 1.5 kg roaster show how cafés can install roasting with no gas lines, no permits, and no construction, handling about 100 lb/week in standard configuration and up to 400 lb/week with a continuous kit (vendor‑reported figures).[^3]

2. Data‑Driven, Sensor‑Rich Roasting

Modern roasting is increasingly a control and data problem. It’s less about manually steering a burner and more about capturing and repeating profiles.

  • Cropster Roast now positions features like machine automation, auto‑start/stop, multiple temperature tracks, and AI‑assisted prediction as core workflow tools.[^4]

  • ROEST P3000 is a 3 kg / 25 kg per hour production roaster that uses 18+ sensors and a live bean camera, finishing roast plus reset in under 7 minutes and requiring roughly 5 minutes of labor per hour, according to ROEST’s own documentation.[^5]

Leading roasters publicly emphasize repeatability:

  • Tim Wendelboe says ROEST can replicate a profile “without human interference.”[^6]

  • Scott Rao calls it the best sample roaster he knows of.[^6]

Together, these point to a market where the best electric commercial coffee roaster is judged by data visibility and consistency, not just mechanical design.

3. Visible, Customer‑Facing Roasting

Roasting is increasingly part of the brand experience. Perfect Daily Grind reports that more roasteries are becoming deliberately customer‑facing because consumers want to observe roasting and “see behind the curtain,” including a Chicago roastery with a 25‑foot glass wall showcasing a 60 kg IMF roaster.[^7]

Typhoon Roasters explicitly built compact shop roasters so customers could experience roasting first‑hand, later opening a Prague showroom where visitors taste coffee roasted on Typhoon machines.[^8] Transparent roasting chambers, compact footprints, and low‑emission electric systems all support the idea of roasting as theatre inside cafés.

Why Electric Roasting Fits Regulatory and Sustainability Pressures

Electrification isn’t just about convenience; it aligns with tightening regulations and sustainability goals.

Air Permits and Emissions (US Context)

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) notes that coffee roasting typically operates at 370–540 °C (698–1004 °F) and uses horizontal rotating drums with hot combustion gases.[^9] Roasting emits particulate matter (PM), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), CO, and CO₂.[^9]

The National Coffee Association (NCA) states that state and local air permits are generally required for most roasting facilities in the US.[^10] While electric roasters still need proper ventilation and afterburning or filtration where required, eliminating on‑site gas combustion can simplify permitting and narrative around emissions.

A 2020 occupational exposure study across 17 roasting/packaging facilities, including 10 cafés, found that flavored production workers had the highest diacetyl and 2,3‑pentanedione exposures, while baristas in cafés had mean full‑shift exposures below recommended limits.[^11] This underscores that process design, flavoring, and ventilation matter more than just heat source—but electric systems can reduce combustion‑related pollutants.

Roast Style and Carbon Emissions

A 2025 MDPI paper reported that light roasting reduced carbon emissions by 33.33% versus dark roasting and 16.67% versus medium roasting in its analysis.[^12]

This doesn’t directly compare electric versus gas, but it shows roast degree itself has a measurable emissions impact.

Electric systems that precisely control profiles can help businesses align roast style with sustainability goals.


Typhoon Roasters’ Vision: Electric, Fluid‑Bed, and Data‑Ready

Typhoon Roasters (Typhoon Coffee) is a European manufacturer of professional electric coffee roasting equipment built around patented fluid‑bed convection technology.[^13] Instead of gas drums, Typhoon uses a controlled stream of hot air to heat the entire bean mass evenly.

100% Convection. 0% Compromise.

Typhoon’s platform is designed for:

  • Defect‑free roasting: Reduced scorching and tipping thanks to even convection and minimal metal‑to‑bean contact.[^13]

  • Faster roast cycles: Vendor‑reported roast times around 5–7 minutes per batch on core models, with up to 6 batches/hour and no dedicated cool‑down cycle.[^14]

  • Energy‑efficient operation: Vendor‑reported energy use around 0.3 kWh per kg across 2.5, 10, 20, and 30 kg systems.[^14]

These figures are based on Typhoon’s internal testing under typical conditions—full or near‑full batch loads, medium roast profiles, and standard preheat routines. As Diedrich has pointed out, without detailed operating conditions, it is impossible to estimate how much energy is actually needed to roast a kilogram on a given machine.[^15] So energy claims across manufacturers should be treated as directional, not perfectly comparable.

Real‑world case data is starting to support Typhoon’s efficiency story. An In Cumbria profile of Penningtons reported that switching to a Typhoon roaster, powered by solar, cut their gas bill from £1,000/month to £100/month while letting them produce twice as much coffee in less than half the time (business‑reported outcome).[^16]

A Single Platform from Café to Factory

Typhoon’s product line covers:

  • Typhoon Shop PRO 2.5 kg and 5 kg – for cafés and micro‑roasteries

  • 10–30 kg industrial systems – up to 120–180 kg/hour continuous production (vendor‑reported).[^^14]

All share:

  • Transparent roasting chambers

  • Fully electric, fluid‑bed convection

  • Advanced automation and recipe storage

  • Fast back‑to‑back batch capability

This means a café can start with a compact commercial coffee roaster for small café use and later scale to industrial capacity without changing core technology.

Typhoon Roasters vs Loring Smart Roast: Sustainability & Performance

Loring Smart Roast is often mentioned alongside Typhoon in discussions of energy‑efficient roasting. Both focus on sustainability, but with different heat and system architectures.

Loring Smart Roast (Gas‑Based, Highly Efficient)

Loring’s systems use a single‑burner, recirculating hot‑air design to reduce gas consumption and emissions compared with classic drum roasters. They’re widely respected for efficiency and cup quality, but they still rely on gas infrastructure and combustion.

Typhoon Roasters (Fully Electric, Fluid‑Bed)

Typhoon’s differentiators versus gas‑based systems like Loring include:[^13][^14]

  • Fully electric: No gas lines, no burners, and easier integration with renewable electricity.

  • Fluid‑bed convection: 100% hot air circulation around the beans, minimizing hot spots.

  • Transparent chambers and compact footprint: Well‑suited to customer‑facing roasting inside cafés.

From a sustainability narrative standpoint:

  • Loring emphasizes reduced gas use and cleaner exhaust.

  • Typhoon emphasizes no gas at all, roughly 3× lower vendor‑reported energy per kg versus some traditional gas drum setups, and compatibility with solar or green grid power.[^14][^16]

Because energy claims vary by operating conditions and measurement methods, businesses should assess both via their own calculations, local energy prices, and any third‑party audits they can access.

Fully Electric Commercial Coffee Roaster Reviews: How Typhoon Compares

When buyers search for fully electric commercial coffee roaster reviews, they’re typically comparing platforms like Typhoon, Bellwether, ROEST, and Coffee Crafters.

Here’s a high‑level, fact‑based look at vendor‑reported specs:

Bellwether Coffee (All‑Electric, No‑Permit Concept)

  • Batch size: 1.5 kg

  • Throughput: ~100 lb/week standard; ~400 lb/week with continuous kit (vendor‑reported)[^3]

  • Energy: Plug‑in 220V; detailed kWh/kg not publicly specified

  • Positioning: No gas, no construction, minimal permitting for many US locations

ROEST P3000 (Production Plus Sample Precision)

  • Batch size: 3 kg

  • Throughput: 25 kg/hour (vendor‑reported)[^5]

  • Sensors: 18+ sensors and live bean camera[^5]

  • Labor: Designed for ~5 minutes of labor per hour[^5]

Coffee Crafters Valenta 18 (Electric Fluid‑Bed)

  • Batch size: 2–18 lb

  • Throughput: 108 lb/hour (vendor‑reported)[^17]

  • Energy: ~0.4 kWh/lb, or about 0.88 kWh/kg[^17]

Typhoon Roasters (Shop PRO and Industrial)

  • Batch size: 2.5–30 kg

  • Throughput: Up to 120–180 kg/hour on larger models (vendor‑reported)[^14]

  • Energy: ~0.3 kWh/kg across models (vendor‑reported)[^14]

  • Design: Transparent, customer‑facing, fully electric fluid‑bed

Again, Diedrich’s caution applies: without identical ambient temperatures, batch sizes, roast degrees, and preheat policies, these energy numbers are signals, not strict benchmarks.[^15] Use them as starting points for ROI modelling, but validate with your own data once the roaster is installed.

Trade‑Offs: Fluid‑Bed vs Drum Roasting

Fluid‑bed roasting has clear strengths but also stylistic trade‑offs compared with classic drums.

Strengths of Fluid‑Bed Systems

  • Faster heat transfer and shorter roast times

  • Even bean development with fewer contact‑related defects

  • Cleaner flavor profile and pronounced clarity, especially at light‑medium roasts

Ben Morrow of Manhattan Coffee Roasters describes Typhoon’s fluid‑bed system as using mostly convection rather than conduction, managed via software and probes, and notes its high energy efficiency.[^18] He moved from a manual Probat drum to a Typhoon electric model, emphasizing how convection supports consistent profiles.

Limitations and Stylistic Differences

Documented and commonly discussed trade‑offs include:

  • Some roasters prefer the heavier body and traditional development curve they associate with drums, especially for classic dark roasts or specific origins.

  • Fluid‑bed systems can produce extremely clean cups that may feel leaner or less "old‑school" to those chasing intense caramelization.

  • For certain high‑density or specific regional coffees, some roasters report needing to adjust their approach when moving from drum to fluid‑bed to achieve desired texture and perceived sweetness.

Because these differences are style‑specific rather than strictly "better vs worse," the best approach is:

  • Run comparative cuppings across your core blends and single origins.

  • Decide whether your brand leans toward clarity and repeatability, or toward traditional profiles that may benefit from drum behavior.

Typhoon’s view is that for specialty cafés emphasizing origin character and consistency, fluid‑bed convection is a strong match.

Checklist: Choosing the Best Electric Coffee Roaster for a Specialty Café

When you’re evaluating the best electric coffee roaster specialty cafe setup, use this checklist.

1. Capacity and Throughput

  • Target weekly volume (kg or lb)

  • Desired batches per hour

  • Growth plans for the next 3–5 years

2. Energy and Electrical Requirements

  • Voltage: Many fully electric commercial roasters require 3‑phase power in the 380–480 V range for larger units; shop roasters may run on 220–240 V single or 3‑phase.

  • Amps: Check manufacturer nameplate; plan for dedicated circuits and margin.

  • Energy modelling: Calculate approximate kWh/week based on vendor figures (e.g., Typhoon’s ~0.3 kWh/kg claim[^14]) and your projected volume.

3. Ventilation and Filtration

Even electric roasters produce smoke and odor. You still need:

  • Proper ducting and exhaust

  • Filters or afterburners where required

  • Compliance with local building codes and air quality regulations

4. Permitting and Jurisdiction Differences

Requirements vary significantly by country, state, and city. In the US:[^10]

  • Most roasting facilities require state/local air permits.

  • Electric roasters can simplify gas‑related permitting but don’t eliminate air rules.

In Europe and other regions, you may face:

  • Local fire and building codes regulating exhaust and placement

  • Occupancy and zoning restrictions for roasting in customer areas

Always consult:

  • Local environmental agencies

  • Fire marshal or building inspector

  • Landlord or property manager

5. Data, Automation, and Integration

To future‑proof your roastery, prioritize:

  • Integration with roast software (e.g., Cropster features: multi‑track logging, machine control, automation[^4])

  • Recipe storage and replay

  • Sensor coverage (bean temperature, exhaust, environmental probes)

A data‑driven coffee roaster with sensor‑rich monitoring will let you scale from one location to many while maintaining cup quality.

6. Customer‑Facing Design

If you want roasting to live in your café:

  • Look for a customer‑facing roaster design with visible chambers.

  • Choose compact footprints suitable for front‑of‑house.

  • Confirm noise levels, heat rejection, and safety features.

Typhoon’s transparent roasting chambers and compact Shop PRO line are designed specifically for this use case.[^8][^13]

Typhoon Roasters Coffee: Preparing Your Business for the Next Decade

Typhoon’s platform is built around three beliefs:[^13]

  1. The future of coffee is electric and efficient. Quality coffee shouldn’t depend on open flames and gas lines.

  2. Consistency is non‑negotiable. Software‑driven profiles and even heat are essential as you scale.

  3. Roasting is part of your brand story. Visible, clean roasting belongs in your café, not just in a factory.

For café owners and roastery startups, this means:

  • You can treat your roaster as both a production engine and an experiential centerpiece.

  • You’re not locked into gas infrastructure as markets and regulations evolve.

  • You can grow from a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster small roastery scenario to industrial output on the same core technology.

FAQ: Electric, Fluid‑Bed, and Customer‑Facing Roasters

What are the best alternatives to gas drum roasters?

The best alternatives to gas drum roasters today include:

  • Fully electric fluid‑bed systems like Typhoon and Coffee Crafters (no gas, convection‑based heat)[^13][^17]

  • Electric shop roasters like Bellwether that emphasize plug‑and‑play installation with minimal construction[^3]

  • Electric hybrid or hot‑air systems from traditional brands (e.g., PROBAT P‑series electrification)[^2]

Your choice depends on required capacity, energy pricing, and whether you prioritize customer‑facing design.

How do fluid‑bed coffee roasters compare for small roasteries?

For small roasteries and cafés, fluid bed coffee roaster recommendations specialty cafe scenarios often favor:

  • Faster roast times and higher hourly throughput

  • Clean, defect‑free cups, especially for light‑medium roasts

  • Easier, software‑led consistency across operators

A commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster small roastery setup, like a Typhoon Shop PRO, can help you roast multiple batches per hour with consistent curves while keeping the roaster visible to customers.[^13][^14]

Are fluid‑bed profiles always better than drum profiles?

No.

They’re different.

Fluid‑bed profiles are often praised for clarity and origin character, while drums can favor heavier body and traditional dark‑roast styles.

Some roasters prefer drum behavior for specific blends or markets.

The best approach is to cup side‑by‑side and decide what fits your brand.


What makes a roaster truly “data‑driven”?

A data‑driven coffee roaster provides:

  • Multiple sensors (bean, exhaust, environment)

  • Real‑time data logging and graphing

  • Recipe storage and automatic profile replay

  • Integration with platforms like Cropster for analysis and automation[^4]

ROEST’s P3000, with its 18+ sensors and automation, is a good example of sensor‑rich design.[^5] Typhoon focuses on software‑driven profiles and repeatable convection curves, aligned with this data‑first direction.[^13][^14]

How do I choose a compact commercial coffee roaster for a small cafe?

When selecting a compact commercial coffee roaster for small cafe use, consider:

  • Footprint and clearance requirements

  • Electrical availability (220–240 V vs 3‑phase)

  • Throughput: can it comfortably handle your peak weekly demand?

  • Visibility: does it support customer‑facing placement?

Typhoon’s smaller Shop PRO units, Bellwether’s plug‑in roaster, and ROEST’s P3000 all target this niche with different trade‑offs in capacity, visibility, and automation.[^3][^5][^13]

Conclusion: Choosing the Best Electric Roaster for Your Café

Electric, data‑driven, and visible roasting is rapidly becoming the new normal for specialty coffee. From PROBAT’s electrified portfolio[^2] to sensor‑rich systems like ROEST[^5] and customer‑facing designs highlighted by Perfect Daily Grind,[^7] the market is clearly moving toward roasters that are smart, efficient, and part of the customer experience.

Typhoon Roasters’ fully electric, fluid‑bed platform is built for that future: defect‑free convection roasting, vendor‑reported 2× faster throughput at roughly 3× lower energy per kg versus many drum systems,[^14] and design language that brings roasting out into the café.

If you’re planning your next roaster purchase, treat it as a strategic decision:

  • Model your capacity, energy, and permitting landscape.

  • Decide how visible you want roasting to be.

  • Prioritize data, automation, and repeatability.

Choosing an electric, sensor‑rich, customer‑facing roaster today—whether Typhoon or another trusted commercial coffee roaster manufacturer—will position your business to thrive in an industry that’s becoming more sustainable, more technical, and more experiential with every roast.

item.title: Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roasting Explained: How Hot Air Changes Your Coffee
item.dc:creator: Typhoon Editorial
item.description: If you’ve only roasted on gas drum machines, fluid‑bed coffee roasting can feel like stepping into a different universe.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve only roasted on gas drum machines, fluid‑bed coffee roasting can feel like stepping into a different universe.

Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roasting Explained: How Hot Air Changes Your Coffee

If you've only roasted on gas drum machines, fluid‑bed coffee roasting can feel like stepping into a different universe.

Instead of a heavy metal drum and open flame, a fluid‑bed roaster uses a controlled stream of hot air to lift, mix, and heat the entire bean mass. The result is:

  • More even heat transfer

  • Fewer roast defects (scorching, tipping, facing)

  • Faster, more repeatable batches

In this guide, we'll demystify fluid‑bed convection roasting, compare it to drum roasting, and show how hot air changes both the roast curve and cup profile—using Typhoon Roasters as practical examples.

What Is Fluid‑Bed Convection Coffee Roasting?

At its core, a fluid‑bed coffee roaster is a 100% convection machine.

Simple definition

  • Fluid‑bed roasting: Beans are suspended and agitated in a rising column of hot air.

  • The bean bed behaves like a "fluid"—constantly moving, with high‑velocity air passing through it.

  • Heat transfer is dominated by convection: hot air touching the beans from all sides.

In Typhoon roasters, patented fluid‑bed technology controls:

  • Air temperature

  • Airflow velocity

  • Bean agitation

This tight control allows roast times of roughly 5–7 minutes per batch with highly repeatable curves.

Key characteristics of fluid‑bed roasting

Fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon share several technical traits:

  • High airflow: Beans are literally lifted and mixed by the air stream.

  • Transparent chamber: Roast is visible to operators and customers (roasting as theatre).

  • Fully electric: No gas lines or burners—Typhoon operates around ~0.3 kWh/kg.

  • Profile storage: Software saves and repeats roast curves batch after batch.

For cafés and small roasteries, this means an electric commercial coffee roaster that fits inside retail spaces and delivers production‑grade consistency.

Fluid‑Bed vs Drum: How Heat Transfer Really Works

To understand why fluid‑bed roasting reduces scorching and tipping, you need to see how heat moves in different machines.

Heat transfer in drum roasting

Traditional drum roasters (Probat, Giesen, etc.) rely mainly on conduction:

  • Beans contact the hot metal drum surface.

  • Heat moves from metal to bean where they touch.
